items.title: Register your employment related securities scheme
items.description: When and how to tell HMRC about new employment related securities (ERS) schemes.
items.changeNote: Updated the 'How to get an agent authorised to submit ERS returns' section with steps to follow to get an agent authorised to use the ERS online service.

ai.summary: Employers must register new tax‑advantaged ERS schemes by 6 July after the tax year they’re set up, and non‑tax‑advantaged schemes by 6 July after the first reportable event. After registration, a return or nil return is due by the same deadline, or penalties may apply.
ai.whoAffected: Employers of SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed owners who run employment‑related securities schemes (tax‑advantaged or non‑tax‑advantaged).
actions: Ensure the client is registered as an employer and obtain a PAYE reference (up to 30 working days).
Enroll and activate the PAYE online service using the PAYE reference and activation code within 28 days.
Register the ERS scheme via HMRC Online Services before the 6 July deadline for the relevant scheme type.
Submit the required ERS return or a nil return by 6 July following the tax year, or authorize an agent to file on their behalf.

items.title: Use a software provider to prepare package accounts for Companies House
items.description: A list of software providers you can use to prepare certain specialist package accounts types, such as audit exempt subsidiary accounts.

ai.summary: The guide lists approved software providers for preparing iXBRL‑tagged ZIP package accounts, required for filing various specialist accounts (CICs, audit‑exempt subsidiaries, limited partnerships, UKSEF, group and Welsh accounts) with Companies House online.
ai.whoAffected: Companies that must file package accounts – e.g., community interest companies, audit‑exempt or dormant subsidiaries, limited partnerships, UKSEF filers, group accounts and Welsh accounts – and the accountants advising them.
actions: Identify which type of package accounts the client needs to file
Select a suitable software provider from the listed options that supports ZIP and iXBRL tagging
Prepare the accounts using the software, ensuring the correct package type is selected
Upload the ZIP file to Companies House via the online filing service
legislationRefs: section 400, parent incorporated under UK law
section 401, parent incorporated under non-UK law

items.title: Tell HMRC your employment related securities scheme has ended
items.description: What you need to do to cease an employment related securities scheme.
items.changeNote: Information has been added about submitting an annual return, including a nil return, after the scheme end date has passed.

ai.summary: Employers must formally end an employment related securities (ERS) scheme by signing into HMRC Online Services, selecting the scheme, providing the final event date and filing any outstanding annual returns (including nil) by 6 July after the tax year ends.
ai.whoAffected: Employers who have registered an employment related securities (ERS) scheme, including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses
actions: Sign in to HMRC Online Services for employers and choose the ‘Employment related Securities’ card
View your schemes, select the one to end and provide the date the scheme stopped
Submit any outstanding ERS annual returns (including a nil return) for the relevant tax year by 6 July following the year‑end
If closing the linked PAYE scheme, ensure the ERS scheme is ended first

items.title: Technical interface specifications for Companies House software
items.description: Technical specifications for developing software to send information to Companies House digitally.
items.changeNote: Edited attachment 'Important information for software developers - read first'. Under heading 'Applying for a test account', the list of what you'll need to tell us when you set up a test account has been updated. And a link to the form to apply for a test account has been added. Also added the latest version of the attachment 'Companies House technical interface specification (TIS) for accounts'.

ai.summary: Technical specs outline XML, iXBRL and zip requirements for software that files company information digitally to Companies House.
ai.whoAffected: Software developers and package accounts filers creating or maintaining Companies House filing applications
actions: Check that the filing software used by the practice complies with the Companies House technical interface specifications
Confirm the software developer has XML (and iXBRL for accounts) expertise as required
Review the file structure and validation rules before submitting filings
Contact xml@companieshouse.gov.uk with any TIS queries

items.title: Benefits for families with more than 2 children before 6 April 2026
items.description: The rules and exceptions that apply if you had more than 2 children before 6 April 2026 and claimed Universal Credit.
items.changeNote: Universal Credit now pays the extra amount for every child. Removed information on when you will receive any increased payment.

ai.summary: From 6 April 2026 the 2‑child limit ends; Universal Credit now pays an extra amount for every child, but extra payments for children born after 6 April 2017 only apply if an exception (multiple birth, adoption, non‑consensual conception, caring arrangement, etc.) is met and count towards the benefit cap.
ai.whoAffected: Clients who claim Universal Credit and have more than two children, especially those with children born before or after 6 April 2017 and any with applicable exceptions (multiple birth, adoption, non‑consensual conception, caring arrangements).
actions: Check each child’s birth date against 6 April 2017 to determine basic entitlement.
Identify any applicable exceptions and collect the required supporting documents.
Advise clients to report any new births or changes in responsibility promptly to DWP.
Use a benefits calculator to see overall entitlement and whether the benefit cap limits the extra child amount.

items.title: Employer Bulletin: October 2026
items.description: A bi-monthly magazine for employers and agents that gives up-to-date information on payroll topics.

ai.summary: The October 2026 Employer Bulletin updates on payrolling benefits in kind exceptions and Class 1A NICs, reminds PSA payments are due by 22 Oct 2026, announces mandatory tax adviser registration opening 18 Nov 2026, outlines trade union law changes, highlights the 2026 Tell ABAB Report and child‑benefit entitlement for parent/carer staff.
ai.whoAffected: Employers, payroll agents and tax advisers; also parent or carer employees
ai.effectiveDate: 22 October 2026 (PSA payment deadline) and 18 November 2026 (tax adviser registration opens)
actions: Tell client employers to make their PAYE Settlement Agreement payment by 22 Oct 2026
Prepare clients for the mandatory tax adviser registration that starts 18 Nov 2026
Review client payroll for benefits‑in‑kind exceptions and Class 1A NIC implications
Inform clients about child‑benefit entitlement for parent/carer employees and recent trade‑union law changes

items.title: Updates on VAT appeals
items.description: Check the list of VAT appeals that HMRC has lost, or partly lost, that could have implications for other businesses.
items.changeNote: The list of VAT appeals that HMRC has lost and that may have implications for other businesses has been updated with 3 additions, 5 amendments and 3 removals.

ai.summary: A regularly updated list shows VAT appeals HMRC has lost or partly lost, which may affect other businesses.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who could be impacted by the precedents set in these appeals
actions: Monitor the HMRC lost‑appeals list for new entries
Assess whether any listed cases are relevant to a client’s VAT position
Advise clients on potential implications and any needed corrective actions
Document any advice and keep records for six months as per the list’s retention period

items.title: Detailed tax guidance for charities
items.description: How to register a charity for tax, charities' tax obligations, and the reliefs and exemptions available.
items.changeNote: ‘Annex ii: non-charitable expenditure’ has been updated to clarify HMRC’s approach to due diligence, record keeping, payments to beneficiaries and overseas bodies. Sections ‘Paying individual beneficiaries’ and ‘Proportionality’ have been added, together with guidance on monitoring the use of charitable funds, maintaining audit trails, and evidencing overseas payments.

ai.summary: Guidance outlines charities' direct and indirect tax duties, reliefs and recent updates on non‑charitable expenditure, due diligence, record‑keeping and overseas payments.
ai.whoAffected: Charities and their trustees
actions: Review the updated Annex ii with charity clients to ensure compliance with due‑diligence and record‑keeping requirements
Check that payments to individual beneficiaries and overseas bodies are properly documented and evidence is retained
Implement audit‑trail procedures for monitoring the use of charitable funds
Confirm that any VAT obligations and reliefs are correctly applied

items.title: Tell HMRC an entity liable for the Economic Crime Levy has become insolvent
items.description: Cancel an organisation or individual's registration for the Economic Crime Levy and send any final returns to HMRC, if they've become insolvent.
items.changeNote: The link to the online form has been updated.

ai.summary: Use HMRC’s online form to submit final Economic Crime Levy returns and cancel registration when a liable organisation or individual becomes insolvent, provided you’re the appointed trustee, liquidator or administrator.
ai.whoAffected: Organisations or individuals liable for the Economic Crime Levy that have entered insolvency, and their appointed trustees, liquidators or administrators.
actions: Gather the required details: name, address, levy registration number, insolvency type, insolvency start date and intended deregistration date.
Confirm you are an authorised party (trustee in bankruptcy, liquidator or administrator).
Sign in to the online form using HMRC credentials or email verification and submit the final returns and cancellation request.
Record the reference number and await HMRC confirmation, noting they will respond within 28 working days.

items.title: VAT refunds for constructing a new charity building
items.description: Check if you can claim a VAT refund using the DIY housebuilders scheme if you’re constructing a new charity building, for a charitable or relevant residential purpose.
items.changeNote: Section ‘Claims rejected or not paid in full’ has been updated with what to do if you think HMRC has missed key information or misunderstood something in your claim.

ai.summary: Charities building new premises for a charitable or relevant residential purpose can claim a VAT refund under the DIY housebuilders scheme, provided the use is at least 95% qualifying. Claims must be submitted within 3 months (pre‑5 Dec 2023) or 6 months (post‑5 Dec 2023) of completion with full documentation.
ai.whoAffected: Charities constructing new buildings for charitable or relevant residential purposes, and any agents authorised to act on their behalf
actions: Confirm the charity is HMRC‑recognised and the building’s use meets the 95% ‘solely’ requirement
Collect all required documents: claim form, invoice schedule, construction evidence, planning permission, building plans and any minor‑use declaration
Submit the claim via the online service or form VAT431NB, optionally authorising an agent using form 64‑8
Track the claim timeline (3 months or 6 months after completion) and respond to HMRC queries or appeal decisions within 30 days

items.title: VAT refunds for new builds if you’re a DIY housebuilder
items.description: Check if you can claim a VAT refund using the DIY housebuilders scheme, if you’re building a new house.
items.changeNote: Section ‘Claims rejected or not paid in full’ has been updated with what to do if you think HMRC has missed key information or misunderstood something in your claim.

ai.summary: DIY housebuilders can claim back VAT on eligible building materials for new residential builds, provided they have planning permission, the property is for personal or family use, and only qualifying goods are purchased.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals or relatives building a new dwelling for residential or holiday use under the DIY housebuilders scheme, including those buying a shell and fitting it out; not applicable to builds intended for sale, letting or other business purposes.
actions: Obtain and submit copies of full or outline planning permission (including any reserved matters) and any Section 106 or Section 75 agreement, keeping originals safe.
Confirm the project meets the definition of a new build and is intended as a family home, not for business or rental use.
Identify only eligible building‑material purchases (exclude furniture, appliances, carpets, garden items, tools, consumables, and land) and ensure VAT was correctly charged on those items.
Prepare the VAT refund claim with the required evidence of lawful works and eligible goods, and submit it to HMRC following the scheme’s guidance.

items.title: Pay money laundering regulations fees
items.description: How to pay money laundering fees, and the time it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Clients must pay money‑laundering supervision fees to HMRC when registering and annually. Payments must use the correct 14‑character reference, be made by the deadline (earlier if weekend/holiday), and can be paid online, by card, or bank transfer. Wrong references cause delays or misallocation.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals required to register for anti‑money laundering supervision (e.g., SMEs, owner‑managed firms, self‑employed)
actions: Obtain and record the 14‑character reference number; email MLRCIT@hmrc.gov.uk if missing
Pay the fee when first applying and at each annual supervision using the correct reference and a suitable method (online, card or bank transfer)
Ensure payment is sent so it reaches HMRC by the end of the previous working day if the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday
If the wrong reference is used, advise the client to contact MLRCIT@hmrc.gov.uk to have the payment moved

items.title: How VAT affects charities (VAT Notice 701/1)
items.description: Find out what a charity is, how VAT affects charities, how to treat a charity's income for VAT and what VAT reliefs a charity can get on what it buys.
items.changeNote: The guidance in ‘Charity acting as an agent’ within section 10 (Charity challenge events) has been updated to show the correct rate of VAT due from the charity as output tax.

ai.summary: VAT Notice 701/1 explains what qualifies as a charity, when charities must register for VAT, the categories of supplies (taxable, exempt, zero‑rated), reliefs on purchases, and rules for trading subsidiaries and VAT groups.
ai.whoAffected: Charities, their trading subsidiaries, businesses that supply to charities, charity fundraisers and users of charity services
actions: Confirm the organisation meets the statutory definition of a charity and has HMRC recognition
Check the charity’s taxable sales against the VAT registration threshold and advise on compulsory or voluntary registration
Identify which of the charity’s purchases qualify for VAT reliefs under Schedule 7A, 8 or 9 and ensure proper documentation
If the charity has a trading subsidiary, assess whether a VAT group registration is beneficial

items.title: Incorporation and names
items.description: Sets out the main requirements for incorporating and naming a company in the UK, including business names and charitable incorporated organisations (CIOs).
items.changeNote: 'Chancery Division of the High Court' has been updated to 'Business and Property Division of the High Court' in Annex B. In Annex A, under heading 'University', subheading 'England and Wales' has been updated to 'England and Wales (except Welsh companies within section 88 Companies Act 2006)'. Subheading 'Wales (a Welsh company as specified in section 88 Companies Act 2006)' has become 'Wales (Welsh companies within section 88 Companies Act 2006)'.

ai.summary: Guide outlines steps to set up a limited company, covering company type, officers, name rules and public disclosure of addresses.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals and entities planning to incorporate a limited company in the UK
actions: Determine the appropriate type of limited company for the client
Identify and record the required company officers
Assist in selecting a company name that meets the stated controls and restrictions
Inform the client that any home address used as a service or registered address will be publicly available

items.title: Making an entry summary declaration
items.description: Make an entry summary declaration if you move goods into Great Britain, into Northern Ireland from Great Britain, or into Northern Ireland from countries outside the EU.
items.changeNote:
Section ‘If you cannot submit declarations’ has been updated to include what you need to provide to identify your declaration.
The file 'Entry summary declaration data elements for the S&S GB service' has been updated.

ai.summary: Carriers must submit an entry summary declaration before goods arrive when moving goods into Great Britain or Northern Ireland, using the S&S GB or ICS2 services, with an appropriate GB or XI/EU EORI, via compatible software or a customs agent.
ai.whoAffected: Carriers (including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed importers) moving goods into Great Britain or Northern Ireland
actions: Check if the goods being moved require an entry summary declaration (imports into GB or NI)
Ensure the client has the correct EORI number (GB for GB imports, XI or EU EORI for NI imports)
Choose a submission method – either self‑submit using compatible XML software or appoint a customs agent/Trader Support Service
Submit the declaration before arrival (up to 200 days in advance) and amend any errors before the goods reach their destination

items.title: Community Amateur Sports Clubs detailed guidance notes
items.description: Find out about how the Community Amateur Sports Club (CASC) scheme works and about reliefs you might be able to benefit from.
items.changeNote: Section 3 updated to include information that CASCs are not eligible to participate in the Payroll Pension Scheme.

ai.summary: The Community Amateur Sports Club (CASC) scheme, introduced in April 2002, lets clubs register with HMRC to claim tax reliefs, but they cannot join the Payroll Pension Scheme.
ai.whoAffected: Community Amateur Sports Clubs
actions: Advise CASC clients to register with HMRC for the scheme
Identify and claim the tax reliefs available to CASCs
Inform clubs they are not eligible for the Payroll Pension Scheme
Monitor updates to the CASC guidance for any changes

items.title: Find payroll software that is recognised by HMRC
items.description: Check for free and paid-for software recognised by HMRC that you can use to report PAYE information online.
items.changeNote: The page has been updated with one removal, 3 additions and 3 amendments.

ai.summary: HMRC recognises a list of free and paid payroll software you can use to report PAYE online; free options apply to businesses with fewer than 10 employees. Choose software based on needed features; HMRC does not endorse any product.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and any employer needing HMRC‑recognised payroll software, especially those with under 10 staff
actions: Determine the client’s employee count and payroll requirements
Check the free HMRC‑recognised software list if the client has fewer than 10 employees
Compare paid‑for software features against the client’s needs using the provided supplier list
Confirm the chosen software is on HMRC’s recognised list before submitting PAYE returns

items.title: Compliance checks: Penalties for digital platform operators — CC/FS98
items.description: This factsheet explains the penalties HMRC may charge digital platform operators for not meeting their reporting obligations.

ai.summary: The factsheet outlines HMRC penalties for digital platform operators who fail to meet reporting duties, where to find registration guidance, rights during penalty considerations, and consequences of providing false information.
ai.whoAffected: Digital platform operators in the UK
actions: Check that the platform is registered with HMRC and understands its reporting obligations
Maintain accurate records to demonstrate compliance with reporting duties
Review the operator’s rights and procedures if HMRC proposes a penalty
Ensure all information supplied to HMRC is truthful and complete

items.title: Chancellor says ‘It is my job to protect resilience of the UK economy and the budget will do that’ in the face of international headwinds
items.description: Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey used the IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok to set out how the UK and its international partners can work together to respond to global economic headwinds and strengthen the conditions for growth.

ai.summary: The Chancellor highlighted the UK’s resilience and announced the upcoming budget will protect growth amid Middle‑East and Ukraine conflicts, rising energy costs, and AI challenges, while promoting international cooperation, G20 leadership and finance for developing economies.
ai.whoAffected: UK households, SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed, plus broader global businesses and developing economies
ai.effectiveDate: early 2027 (announced priorities for the G20 presidency)
actions: Monitor the Chancellor’s budget announcements for fiscal measures affecting SMEs
Advise clients on AI adoption, identifying barriers and risk management
Prepare clients for potential energy price impacts and borrowing cost changes
Stay updated on G20 finance track outcomes that may influence international finance opportunities

items.title: How to make a voluntary disclosure to HMRC
items.description: Find out about the different ways to make a voluntary disclosure to HMRC if you think you have not paid the correct amount of tax.
items.changeNote: The section ‘Ways to make a disclosure’ has been updated to explain errors you should correct and information to provide when making a disclosure, and what to do when you should have treated a worker as an employee for tax purposes.

ai.summary: If you owe tax on income or gains, you must inform HMRC immediately about any unpaid tax. This guide outlines how to make a voluntary disclosure.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed, who have unpaid tax on income or gains
actions: Identify any unpaid tax on income or gains
Contact HMRC promptly to disclose the unpaid tax
Gather details of the tax owed and the period involved
Submit the voluntary disclosure using HMRC’s preferred method (online, phone or written)

items.title: CWG2: further guide to PAYE and National Insurance contributions
items.description: Find out about detailed Pay As You Earn (PAYE) and National Insurance contributions for current and previous years if you're an employer.
items.changeNote: HTML document ‘2026 to 2027: Employer further guide to PAYE and National Insurance contributions’ has been updated in section 5.4.2 to reflect the new 'car or van' hire rate from 44 percent per mile to 55 percent per mile,

ai.summary: The guide explains PAYE and NIC handling in less common cases and notes the car/van hire rate has been updated to 55% per mile.
ai.whoAffected: Employers, including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses, that operate PAYE/NIC and have car or van hire arrangements
actions: Check client records for car/van hire mileage calculations
Apply the new 55% per mile rate for hire vehicles
Adjust PAYE and NIC computations accordingly
Review the guide for any other uncommon PAYE/NIC issues affecting clients

items.title: Ask your employer for Statutory Sick Pay
items.description: You can use the SC2 form to ask your employer for Statutory Sick Pay (SSP).

ai.summary: Use the online SC2 form to self‑certify a sick absence and claim Statutory Sick Pay; you must be off work at least one full working day and provide your NI number, contact details, sickness dates, last working day and payroll number.
ai.whoAffected: Employees who are off work sick and need to claim Statutory Sick Pay from their employer
actions: Check the employee’s contract for any specific sickness procedures
Confirm the employee has been off work for at least one full working day
Gather required details: NI number, phone, sickness dates, last working day before sickness, payroll number
Complete the online SC2 form, give it to the employer and keep a copy

items.title: Agent update: issue 148
items.description: Get guidance from HMRC if you're a tax agent or an adviser

ai.summary: Agent updates provide guidance and news for tax agents and advisers, covering topics like tax, Making Tax Digital, HMRC services and engagement, with the next edition due in November 2026.
ai.whoAffected: Tax agents and advisers
actions: Read this month’s Agent Update highlights
Mark November 2026 for the next edition
Sign up for email reminders for future editions
Distribute relevant updates to your client‑base

items.title: Check the recognised overseas pension schemes notification list
items.description: Find schemes that have told HMRC they meet the conditions to be a recognised overseas pension scheme (ROPS).
items.changeNote: The recognised overseas pension schemes notification list has been updated with 25 schemes added, 17 schemes removed and one scheme amended.

ai.summary: The ROPS list, updated twice monthly, shows schemes claiming recognised overseas pension status, but HMRC does not guarantee tax‑free transfers. Advisors must verify tax liability and monitor list changes before any pension move.
ai.whoAffected: SME owners, self‑employed individuals and their advisers considering overseas pension transfers
ai.effectiveDate: Published on the 1st and 15th of each month (or the next working day if a weekend or UK public holiday)
actions: Check the latest ROPS notification list before advising any overseas pension transfer
Confirm the tax treatment of the transfer with HMRC or a qualified financial adviser
Monitor the list for short‑notice removals or amendments up to the transfer date
Maintain documentation in case HMRC pursues tax charges, interest or penalties

items.title: Find out which HMRC services are experiencing issues
items.description: Find out which HMRC services are currently experiencing unplanned downtime.

ai.summary: The page reports that no HMRC services are currently experiencing unplanned downtime.
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source
actions: Monitor this page regularly for any unplanned downtime updates
Visit the HMRC service availability and issues page for information on planned downtime
Inform clients to check these sources before filing or making payments
Advise clients that, at present, no unplanned service disruptions are reported

items.title: Declare goods that you're moving to or from Northern Ireland using the Trader Support Service (TSS)
items.description: Sign in to make and manage movements of goods to or from Northern Ireland and get support with your declarations and payments.

ai.summary: The free Trader Support Service (TSS) lets businesses and hauliers make customs, safety and security declarations for movements between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, access guidance, check balances, make payments and manage account users. Registration is required, and existing users need an invitation to add new users.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed hauliers that move goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, or make customs declarations on their own or for others
actions: Advise clients to register for the Trader Support Service before moving goods
Ensure clients have their sign‑in details and, if needed, request an invitation from the account administrator
Help clients use TSS to draft and submit customs, safety and security declarations
Assist clients in checking balances, making duty payments and managing user permissions

items.title: Pay duty on biofuels or road fuel gas
items.description: How to pay duty on biofuels or road fuel gas, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Duty on biofuels or road fuel gas must be paid by the 15th day after each return period using the correct X‑prefixed reference; late payments can incur penalties. Various payment methods are available, each with specific processing times, and wrong references may delay or misallocate funds.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that produce, import or use biofuels or gas for road vehicles, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed operators who must file returns and pay the associated duty.
actions: Submit the return and pay any duty by the 15th day after the end of the return period, ensuring it reaches HMRC before the deadline if the 15th falls on a weekend or bank holiday.
Check that you are using the correct 15‑character payment reference (XMBF for biofuels, XMGR for road fuel gas) to avoid delays or misallocation.
Choose a payment method that meets the timing requirements (e.g., Direct Debit – allow 10 working days, Bacs – allow 3 working days, CHAPS/Faster Payments – same or next day) and verify bank limits.
If the wrong reference is used, email morc.exciseenquiries@hmrc.gov.uk to request the payment be moved to the correct tax account.

items.title: Seven linked companies shut down after Insolvency Service investigation with Companies House
items.description: The companies appeared unrelated until a joint investigation uncovered similar conduct concerns.
items.changeNote: Removed address details for Kevin Steven Fryer Ltd.

ai.summary: Seven companies were wound up by the High Court after the Insolvency Service and Companies House uncovered false filings, misleading audit information and no genuine trading presence, highlighting the risk of non‑compliance for small firms.
ai.whoAffected: Directors and owners of SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and other companies that file at Companies House, plus anyone relying on the register for business decisions.
actions: Check that all accounts and audit statements filed at Companies House are accurate and can be verified by the audit firm
Ensure the registered office address is a genuine, occupied location and is kept up to date
Maintain clear records of actual trading activity to demonstrate a real business presence
Co‑operate fully with any regulator or Insolvency Service enquiries

items.title: Pay the VAT due on your One Stop Shop VAT Return
items.description: How to pay the VAT due on your One Stop Shop VAT (OSS) Return and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: The payment reference to use when paying by bank transfer has been updated.

ai.summary: OSS VAT returns must be submitted and the VAT paid in full by the last day of the month after each quarter; payments can be made online, by card, or bank transfer using the pre‑populated NI reference, with specific processing times and penalties for late or incorrect payments.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses registered for the One Stop Shop (OSS) VAT scheme, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed.
actions: Ensure the OSS VAT return is filed and payment is made by the last day of the month following the quarter (or the previous working day if the deadline falls on a weekend/holiday).
Confirm the 11‑character NI payment reference is used; an incorrect reference can delay or misallocate the payment.
Choose a payment method and allow for its processing time (instant/2 hrs for online bank approval, same/next day for CHAPS/Faster Payments, 3 working days for BACS).
If payment issues arise, advise the client to contact HMRC at paymentteam.moss@hmrc.gov.uk for assistance.

items.title: Pay Air Passenger Duty
items.description: How to pay Air Passenger Duty, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Guide explains when Air Passenger Duty must be paid, how to use the correct 15‑character reference, payment methods (online, Direct Debit, CHAPS, Faster Payments, Bacs, cheque) and deadlines, including extensions and penalties for late payment.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and operators that owe Air Passenger Duty, including occasional operators and any entity filing a return with HMRC.
actions: Confirm the client has the 15‑character reference number starting with X and record it for each payment
Check the filing deadline and remind the client to pay by the due date, using the 7‑day extension if paying by Direct Debit, Faster Payments, CHAPS or Bacs
Select an appropriate payment method and advise on processing times (instant/2 hrs for online, same/next day for CHAPS/Faster Payments, 3 days for Bacs)
If the wrong reference is used, instruct the client to email APDHelpdesk@hmrc.gov.uk to request the payment be moved

items.title: Joint and several liability — penalties charged for facilitating avoidance or evasion — JAS/FS3
items.description: This factsheet gives information about whether you may be jointly and severally liable for the relevant tax liability of a company that has been charged penalties for facilitating avoidance or evasion.
items.changeNote: The 'Conditions for giving a joint liability notice' section has been updated to include additional provisions under 'Condition A'.

ai.summary: Not stated in source
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source

items.title: Apply for an agent services account
items.description: Apply for an agent services account (ASA) to register with HMRC as a tax adviser and use certain HMRC services.
items.changeNote: The link to check the progress of an existing application has been updated.

ai.summary: Tax advisers who are paid to handle others’ tax affairs must apply for an Agent Services Account, providing Gateway IDs, UTR, registration numbers and proof of AML supervision, then use the account to interact with HMRC on clients’ behalf.
ai.whoAffected: Tax advisers dealing with other people’s tax affairs for payment
actions: Gather required details: business and personal Government Gateway IDs, UTR, postcode, company/VAT numbers, AML supervisory body name and proof of supervision
Confirm AML supervision is approved before applying
Sign in to Government Gateway and submit the Agent Services Account application
After approval, create individual staff Gateway IDs, set permissions and use the account to act for clients

items.title: More than 600,000 families conjure up Hallowe’en savings with Tax-Free Childcare
items.description: Working families urged to sign up to Tax-Free Childcare to save on their childcare costs.

ai.summary: Tax-Free Childcare lets working families save up to £2,000 per child annually (or £4,000 if disabled) with a government top‑up of £2 for every £8 deposited. Eligibility requires children under 11 (or under 16 if disabled), earnings at least minimum wage and under £100k, and no Universal Credit or vouchers.
ai.whoAffected: Working parents (including self‑employed) with children aged 11 or under (or up to 16 if disabled), earning at least the National Minimum or Living Wage and no more than £100,000, who do not receive Universal Credit or childcare vouchers; also childcare providers who wish to receive payments via the scheme.
actions: Check client eligibility (child age, earnings, benefit status)
Help client register a separate Tax-Free Childcare account for each eligible child on GOV.UK
Explain the government top‑up (£2 for every £8 deposited) and how savings can be used for approved childcare
Remind client to confirm details every 3 months to keep receiving the top‑up

items.title: Sign up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: If you're a sole trader or landlord, use the online service to sign up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
items.changeNote: The option to prove your identity by answering questions has been removed.

ai.summary: Sole traders and landlords with self‑employment or property turnover over £50,000 must sign up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax by 6 April 2026, using compatible software to send quarterly updates and a Self Assessment return. HMRC will auto‑enrol from September 2026 if not signed up.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders, landlords and their agents whose combined self‑employment and property income exceeds £50,000; also anyone who may be exempt or whose income has ceased must confirm their status.
ai.effectiveDate: From 6 April 2026 for required users; HMRC will begin auto‑enrolments in September 2026 for the 2026‑2027 tax year.
actions: Check client’s qualifying self‑employment and property income against the £50,000 threshold using the previous year’s tax return
Confirm the client is registered for Self Assessment and has filed a return in the last two years
Ensure the client has compatible Making Tax Digital software and advise on keeping digital records and sending quarterly updates
If not already signed up, either sign the client up as an agent or guide them to sign up before September 2026, and verify any exemptions or ceased income are reported

items.title: Filing your Company Tax Return online
items.description: Find recognised commercial software suppliers and software you can use to file your Company Tax Return and any supplementary pages online.
items.changeNote: The list of commercial software suppliers for Corporation Tax has been updated with one addition to the ‘Produce and Submit CT600’ and ‘iXBRL integrated Software Application providers’ sections.

ai.summary: Companies must file their Corporation Tax return online using HMRC‑approved commercial software; paper returns are only allowed with a reasonable excuse or in Welsh. The software can also produce iXBRL accounts and may file annual accounts together.
ai.whoAffected: Companies required to file a Company Tax Return, including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses
actions: Identify a recognised commercial software supplier from HMRC's list
Prepare the CT600 and iXBRL accounts using the software
Submit the return online unless you have a reasonable excuse or need to file in Welsh
If desired, file annual accounts together via the software or separately with Companies House

items.title: Approved offshore reporting funds
items.description: Find a list of offshore funds that have applied for and been approved as reporting funds.
items.changeNote: The list of reporting funds has been updated.

ai.summary: A monthly‑updated list shows offshore funds approved by HMRC as reporting funds, including their reference numbers and identification codes.
ai.whoAffected: Offshore funds and advisers/clients who need to confirm reporting‑fund status
actions: Check the HMRC‑approved reporting fund list each month
Match client offshore fund references to the list entries
Confirm that client funds have reporting fund status for compliance
Record the fund identifiers (ISIN, SEDR, CUSIP) for client files

items.title: Corporation Tax technical specifications for CT600 RIM artefacts
items.description: CT600 V3 (2027), CT600 V3 (2026) and CT600 V2 (2009) RIM artefacts for Corporation Tax software developers.
items.changeNote: 'CT600 V3 (2026) Artefacts V1.995' has been renamed to 'CT600 V3 (2027) Artifacts V1.995'.

ai.summary: CT600 V3 (2027) artefacts version V1.995 released 25 Sept 2026, pending implementation in LTS, TPVS and live; earlier versions already live.
ai.whoAffected: Corporation Tax software developers (and firms using their software)
actions: Check that your corporation tax software is prepared for CT600 V3 (2027) artefacts V1.995
Confirm the artefacts are still awaiting implementation in LTS, TPVS and live
Plan to update software once the artefacts move to live status
Inform SME/owner‑managed clients of upcoming filing changes

items.title: Request your employment history from National Insurance records
items.description: Use this form if you need confirmation of your employment history to make a claim for compensation.
items.changeNote: The employment history form has been updated with a new return address.

ai.summary: Use the updated form to request HMRC confirmation of employment history when making a compensation claim for industrial injury, personal injury, medical negligence or other causes.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals filing compensation claims (including employees and self‑employed) who need proof of their employment history
actions: Identify the client’s need for an employment‑history record for a compensation claim
Obtain the latest employment‑history form with the new return address
Complete and submit the form to HMRC on the client’s behalf
Monitor the request and provide the client with the received confirmation

items.title: Find out about the loan charge settlement scheme
items.description: Find out about settling your outstanding disguised remuneration loan charge liability under the loan charge settlement scheme.
items.changeNote: A link to ‘How HMRC will implement the loan charge settlement scheme’ has been added to the section ‘What the settlement scheme includes’.

ai.summary: The loan charge settlement scheme lets individuals or employers with unpaid disguised remuneration liabilities settle their tax, NIC and reduced fees, offering up to £70,000 reduction, a £5,000 extra cut, and exclusion of most penalties, but not late interest or Inheritance Tax beyond a short window.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals and employers who have a disguised remuneration loan charge liability that has not been paid in full, including any related Inheritance Tax liabilities arising from loan‑charge trusts.
actions: Check the client’s loan charge liability letter to confirm they have been identified as eligible for the settlement scheme.
Compare the figures in the settlement offer with the client’s records and discuss any discrepancies with the HMRC caseworker.
If the client cannot pay the full amount, contact the caseworker to arrange an instalment payment plan (up to five years) and explain the interest implications.
Assist the client in completing, signing and returning the acceptance form (by post or scanned email) and advise them to seek independent professional advice if needed.

items.title: Pay tax as a pension scheme administrator
items.description: How to pay charges on payments from registered pension schemes and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Pension scheme administrators must submit returns and pay any tax within 45 days of the tax period end, using the correct 14‑character reference. Payments can be made online, by bank transfer, cheque or Government Banking Service, but wrong references or missed deadlines can cause delays, penalties or interest.
ai.whoAffected: Pension scheme administrators of registered pension schemes, including managers of overseas schemes and government departments using the Government Banking Service
actions: Ensure client returns and any tax are filed within 45 calendar days of the tax period end (or by 31 January for reportable events)
Check the 14‑character reference starts with X and matches the HMRC record before paying
Choose a payment method and confirm processing times (e.g., CHAPS/Faster Payments same‑day, Bacs 3 days)
Record the payment reference and date, and monitor for confirmation to avoid penalties

items.title: HMRC videos and webinars for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: Learn more about Making Tax Digital for Income Tax if you're an agent, sole trader or landlord.
items.changeNote: The recorded webinar link for 'Making Tax Digital if you are a landlord and joint property owner' and the video 'How to sign up your clients to Making Tax Digital for Income Tax' have been updated.

ai.summary: HMRC provides videos, webinars and guidance to help sole traders, landlords and agents prepare for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, including software choice, registration, authorisations and digital record‑keeping, with mandatory use starting from 6 April 2026 for higher‑income earners.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders, landlords (including joint owners), agents and their self‑employed or property‑income clients, plus any small business with qualifying income
actions: Identify clients whose income exceeds the thresholds and note the applicable start dates
Recommend HMRC‑recognised compatible software that covers all their income streams
Assist clients in registering, authorising the agent services account and signing up for MTD
Set up digital record‑keeping and quarterly update processes

items.title: Starting early is key to less stress around Self Assessment
items.description: Customers encouraged to start their Self Assessment tax return well ahead of the 31 January deadline.

ai.summary: HMRC urges Self Assessment customers to start their returns early to reduce anxiety, offering online guidance, a checker tool and tips like preparing records, filing in stages, budgeting payments and using digital services. Key deadlines are 31 Oct 2026 for paper and 31 Jan 2027 for online returns.
ai.whoAffected: Self Assessment taxpayers, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses, the self‑employed, PAYE earners, those receiving Winter Fuel or Pension Age Winter Heating Payments, and High Income Child Benefit Charge payers
ai.effectiveDate: Paper return deadline 31 Oct 2026; online return deadline 31 Jan 2027 (2025‑2026 tax year)
actions: Advise clients to gather all records and start the return early, using GOV.UK guidance
Encourage use of the Self Assessment checker tool to confirm filing requirement and register if needed
Recommend filing online before 30 Dec 2026 for PAYE clients and budgeting payments (e.g., monthly instalments)
Highlight digital options such as Making Tax Digital for Income Tax and the HICBC PAYE service for eligible clients
legislationRefs: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

items.title: Pay General Betting, Pool Betting or Remote Gaming Duty
items.description: How to pay General Betting, Pool Betting or Remote Gaming Duty, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Guide explains when and how to pay General Betting, Pool Betting and Remote Gaming Duty, including deadlines (30 days after each accounting period), required 14‑character reference, payment methods (online, card, bank transfer, cheque) and steps if wrong reference is used.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that operate remote gambling, general betting or pool betting and are liable for the respective duties, including owners of SMEs and self‑employed gambling operators.
actions: Confirm the client has the correct 14‑character reference number (starts with X) from HMRC online services.
Submit the duty return and ensure payment is made within 30 days of the accounting period end, reaching HMRC by the previous working day if the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday.
Choose an appropriate payment method (online bank approval, debit/corporate card, CHAPS/Faster Payments, Bacs or cheque) and follow the timing guidance for each method.
If the wrong reference is used, advise the client to contact Gambling duties enquiries promptly to request the payment be moved.

items.title: Pay Insurance Premium Tax
items.description: How to pay Insurance Premium Tax, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Insurers must file their IPT return by the deadline and pay using the correct 15‑character reference. Payments can be made via Direct Debit, Faster Payments, CHAPS, BACS, online banking, cheque or overseas transfer, observing method‑specific processing times.
ai.whoAffected: Insurers liable for Insurance Premium Tax, including overseas insurers using agents, and any business that has an IPT liability
actions: Verify the 15‑character reference (starting with X) from the registration certificate or notice to file before paying
Choose a payment method that meets the deadline and allow the required processing time (10 days for Direct Debit setup, 3 days for BACS)
If the wrong reference is used, contact Insurance Premium Tax enquiries promptly to have the payment moved
Submit the return even when no tax is due

items.title: How to get authorised to act as a tax agent on behalf of your clients
items.description: Find out the different ways you can get client authorisation including the digital handshake, Online Agent Authorisation service, paper forms and through your client's business tax account.
items.changeNote: The 'Find out the different ways to get client authorisation' section has been updated to remove 'Online Tax Registration Service' as a way to get client authorisation.

ai.summary: After registering as a tax agent you must obtain client authorisation before transacting. Choose the method that matches each tax service—digital handshake, Online Agent Authorisation, business tax account or paper form (e.g., 64‑8). Do not use the client’s HMRC sign‑in details.
ai.whoAffected: Tax agents and their SME, owner‑managed and self‑employed clients who need authorisation to act on tax matters
actions: Register as a tax agent with HMRC
Select the appropriate authorisation method for each tax service (digital handshake, Online Agent Authorisation, client’s business tax account or the relevant paper form)
If the client is digitally excluded, give them the authorisation request link and HMRC contact number
Never use the client’s HMRC sign‑in details; obtain formal authorisation instead

items.title: Check the identity of someone representing HMRC in person
items.description: How to verify the identity of an HMRC officer or an HMRC collector if they contact you in person.
items.changeNote: The process to confirm the identity of an HMRC officer when meeting them in person has been updated.

ai.summary: When an HMRC officer or collector visits in person, ask to see their ID card, record the name and serial number, then call the provided HMRC verification number to confirm their identity. Use the number only for verification, not general enquiries.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who may receive face‑to‑face visits from HMRC officers or collectors
actions: Ask the visitor to show their HMRC identification card and note name and serial number
Call the appropriate HMRC verification line (03000 565 656 for officers, 0300 200 3862 for collectors) and give the details
If the visit is outside 8 am‑6 pm Mon‑Fri, arrange a later appointment before confirming identity
Do not use the verification number for any other HMRC enquiries

items.title: Check the identity of someone representing HMRC in person
items.description: How to verify the identity of an HMRC officer or an HMRC collector if they contact you in person.
items.changeNote: The process to confirm the identity of an HMRC officer when meeting them in person has been updated.

ai.summary: To verify an in‑person HMRC officer or collector, ask for their ID card, note name and serial number, then call the dedicated verification line to confirm they are genuine; use only for identity checks, not general queries.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed who may receive in‑person visits from HMRC officers or collectors
actions: Ask the visitor to show their HMRC identification card and record the name and serial number
Call the appropriate verification number (03000 565 656 for officers, 0300 200 3862 for collectors) and provide the recorded details
Use the verification line only to confirm identity, not for general enquiries
If a collector visits outside 8 am‑6 pm Mon‑Fri, arrange an appointment within those hours before confirming identity

items.title: Compliance checks: prohibition of promotion of certain tax avoidance schemes — CC/FS91
items.description: This factsheet tells you about what happens if you promote certain tax avoidance schemes.

ai.summary: The factsheet explains the rules against promoting certain tax avoidance schemes, defines promotion and arrangements, outlines civil and criminal penalties, rights during penalty considerations, how to dispute penalties, and where to get help.
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source
actions: Check that your practice does not promote any prohibited tax avoidance schemes
Familiarise yourself with HMRC’s definitions of “promote” and “arrangements”
Put in place procedures to respond if HMRC considers imposing penalties
Seek HMRC guidance or professional advice if you receive a penalty notice

items.title: Companies House accessibility statements
items.description: These accessibility statements apply to service subdomains run by Companies House.
items.changeNote: Added an English and Welsh language accessibility statement for the Companies House Webchat service.

ai.summary: Companies House provides separate accessibility statements for each of its services, detailing how accessible they are, how to report issues, and the dates the statements were prepared and last tested.
ai.whoAffected: Users of Companies House services, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Review the accessibility statement for each Companies House service your clients use
Note the reported accessibility level and any identified issues
Follow the provided procedure to report any problems encountered
Record the statement preparation and last test dates for compliance tracking

items.title: Apply for an increase in tax credits for a backdated disability benefit decision
items.description: Ask for a backdated disability benefit decision to be included in a period when you were claiming Working Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit.

ai.summary: If a client receives a backdated disability benefit while claiming Working Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit, they can request extra tax credits. Apply within one month using the appropriate HMRC form (adult TC‑DB1 or child TC‑DB2) and follow the submission instructions.
ai.whoAffected: People who have received a backdated disability benefit decision during a period when they were claiming Working Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit
actions: Check the client meets the conditions in helpsheet TC956
Ensure the application is submitted within one month of notification of the backdated benefit
Obtain the correct form (TC‑DB1 for adults or TC‑DB2 for children), complete it in Adobe Reader, save and email it to HMRC
Warn the client that providing false information can lead to a fine up to £3,000 and that HMRC will verify the claim and inform them of any payment

items.title: Approved payers in the middleman scheme
items.description: Check this list of approved payers for non-UK resident entertainers and find out if you need to deduct withholding tax.
items.changeNote: The list of approved payers in the middleman scheme has been updated with one removal.

ai.summary: Payments to non‑UK resident entertainers over the personal allowance require withholding tax unless the payer is on the approved middleman scheme list.
ai.whoAffected: UK businesses and self‑employed individuals who pay non‑UK resident entertainers for appearances or performances in the UK
actions: Determine if the payment exceeds the personal tax allowance
Check the approved payer list to see if the payer is part of the middleman scheme
If the payer is not approved, deduct the required withholding tax
If the payer is approved, no withholding tax is needed and retain evidence of the check

items.title: Authorising an agent to deal with your tax affairs
items.description: Check what a paid agent can do on your behalf. How you authorise the agent depends on the tax, and you may need to use paper form 64-8 or an online service.
items.changeNote: Information about a new online tool to find more guidance about VAT has been added to the VAT section of what an authorised agent can do on your behalf.

ai.summary: The guide explains how to authorise a paid agent for various UK taxes, outlining what agents can do, the forms (64-8, COMP1a) and online methods required, and stresses the taxpayer’s ongoing legal responsibility and need to review submissions.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses, self‑employed individuals and anyone using a paid accountant or tax adviser to handle their HMRC affairs
actions: Identify the specific tax services the client needs an agent for (e.g., Self Assessment, VAT, Corporation Tax).
Choose the appropriate authorisation method – online service or the 64‑8 form – and complete it with correct agent codes.
Ensure the client reviews and confirms any returns or submissions before the agent files them with HMRC.
Maintain a record of the authorisation and promptly change or remove it when the relationship ends

items.title: Tell HMRC the value of items in your PAYE Settlement Agreement
items.description: Use form PSA1 or send an informal calculation to tell HMRC about the value of items included in your PAYE Settlement Agreement.
items.changeNote: Made it clearer that you need to tell HMRC the value of items in your PAYE Settlement Agreement even if you did not provide any benefits or expenses to employees (a nil return).

ai.summary: Employers or agents must report the value of benefits or expenses in a PAYE Settlement Agreement to HMRC, even if none were provided (a nil return).
ai.whoAffected: Employers, agents and businesses that operate PAYE Settlement Agreements, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed employers.
actions: Gather email, tax year, PAYE reference and applicable tax rates for all employees (including those below the personal allowance).
Submit the values using the online PSA1 form via Government Gateway or email confirmation code.
If preferred, send an informal written calculation to HMRC’s PAYE Settlement Agreements address, noting it may take longer to process.
Ensure all employees who received benefits or expenses are included, even when reporting a nil return.

items.title: Real Time Information internet submissions: 2027 to 2028 technical specifications
items.description: Real Time Information (RTI) Rules and Interface Management (RIM) artefacts and supporting technical specifications for software developers.
items.changeNote: 'RTI data item guide 2027 to 2028 v1.1' has been added.

ai.summary: Test service support for RTI internet submissions starts in October 2026, with the live service launching in March 2027.
ai.whoAffected: Software developers of RTI submission tools and payroll service providers serving SMEs and the self‑employed
actions: Begin testing against the RTI test service from October 2026
Review the technical specifications to ensure compliance
Update payroll software before the March 2027 live launch
Inform clients of upcoming changes and timelines

items.title: Local reference rents, listed by BRMA and property size (September 2026)
items.description: Local reference rent (LRR) levels by number of rooms and broad rental market areas (BRMA) for residential properties in England in September 2026.

ai.summary: The publication lists local reference rent (LRR) levels for residential properties in England by room count and Broad Rental Market Area (BRMA) for September 2026, and defines the BRMA and category terms.
ai.whoAffected: Landlords, property owners, letting agents, tenants and anyone dealing with Housing Benefit calculations in England
actions: Check the LRR tables for the relevant BRMA and room category when advising on rent levels
Apply the correct CAT 1A, 1B or 1C definition to each property
Consult the Housing Benefit referral section of the Rent Officer Handbook for detailed LRR calculations
Refer to the National Archives for previous LRR releases if historical comparison is needed

items.title: Check if you need to pay tax when you sell cryptoassets
items.description: Find out if you need to pay Capital Gains Tax on gains you make when you sell, exchange or give away cryptoasset tokens (like bitcoin, XRP or ether).
items.changeNote: The video about how cryptoassets are taxed for individuals has been updated.

ai.summary: You may owe Capital Gains Tax when you sell, exchange, spend or give away cryptoasset tokens. Calculate gains per transaction using pooling (except same‑day or within 30 days), deduct allowable costs, report if total gains exceed the CGT allowance, and keep full records.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals—including SME owners, self‑employed and other taxpayers—who dispose of cryptoasset tokens by selling, exchanging, using for purchases or gifting (except to spouse, civil partner or charity).
actions: Identify each cryptoasset disposal and calculate the gain using the pooling rules, noting any same‑day or 30‑day exceptions.
Deduct allowable costs and any capital losses, then total the gains for the tax year.
If total gains exceed the Capital Gains Tax allowance, report the gain on a Self Assessment return or via the CGT real‑time service and pay the tax due.
Maintain detailed records for each token pool: transaction dates, amounts, values in GBP, bank statements and pooled cost calculations.
legislationRefs: Capital Gains Tax real time service

items.title: Check if you have to pay tax on your pension
items.description: Use this tool to calculate how much Income Tax you may need to pay when you get a pension.
items.changeNote: Tool updated to provide an estimate of Income Tax you may need to pay when you get a pension.

ai.summary: The gov.uk tool estimates whether an individual must pay Income Tax on their State or private pension for the current tax year, based on the standard Personal Allowance and other taxable income, excluding foreign income and Blind Person’s Allowance.
ai.whoAffected: Anyone receiving a State Pension or private pension, including self‑employed, SME owners and other individuals with pension income
actions: Collect details of the client’s State and private pension amounts
Gather information on any other taxable income and Marriage Allowance status
Enter the data into the government pension tax tool to get an estimate
Discuss the estimate with the client and advise on any tax planning needed

items.title: Sole traders and landlords earning more than £30,000 urged to act now
items.description: Sole traders and landlords earning over £30,000 urged to get ready for Making Tax Digital.

ai.summary: From 6 April 2027 sole traders and landlords with turnover over £30,000 must use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, requiring digital records and quarterly updates via compatible software.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders and landlords whose turnover exceeds £30,000 and who are registered for Self Assessment.
actions: Verify each client’s turnover exceeds £30,000 (gross income before allowances).
Confirm they are registered for Self Assessment and have filed a return in the past two years.
Register them on GOV.UK for MTD for Income Tax and select HMRC‑recognised software.
Set up quarterly digital record‑keeping so updates can be sent on time.

items.title: Tell HMRC about an ending of a conditional exemption (IHT100f)
items.description: Use this form to tell us about an event affecting property with an exemption from Inheritance Tax or Estate Duty.
items.changeNote: A new version of 'How to fill in form IHT100f' has been added with updated information on the declaration.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100f to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due and follow the online completion steps.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals or estates that need to report Inheritance Tax due
actions: Download and save form IHT100f to your computer
Open the form using the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form won’t open, contact online services support

items.title: Check if you meet HMRC's conditions to register as a tax adviser
items.description: Check if you meet the conditions to register with HMRC and interact on behalf of your clients.
items.changeNote: Updates have been made to section 'Who needs to meet the conditions' and 'The registration conditions'.

ai.summary: If you charge for dealing with HMRC on clients' tax affairs, you must register for an agent services account, prove AML supervision, and ensure your business and its relevant individuals meet specific conditions, including no outstanding tax, sanctions, or disqualifications.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that provide paid tax‑advice services and any officers (relevant individuals) of those businesses, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed advisers.
actions: Check whether your paid tax‑advice activities require registration with HMRC.
Identify relevant individuals – all officers if ≤5, or select at least five officers if >5, based on strategic tax‑advice roles.
Obtain and retain evidence of approved anti‑money‑laundering supervision before applying.
Apply for an agent services account and be prepared to supply additional evidence if HMRC requests it.

items.title: PAYE internet submissions, expenses and benefits — schema 2026 to 2027
items.description: The PAYE internet submissions, expenses and benefits schema and supporting documents for PAYE software developers.

ai.summary: The PAYE internet submissions, expenses and benefits schema for 2026‑27 is released, with test service support starting October 2026 and the live service commencing in April 2027.
ai.whoAffected: PAYE software developers
actions: Review the new PAYE schema and supporting documents
Begin testing against the PAYE test service from October 2026
Update any PAYE software to meet the new schema before the live service
Inform clients of the April 2027 live service start date

items.title: Tell HMRC about a gift or other transfers of value in a trust (IHT100a)
items.description: Use this form to tell us that Inheritance Tax is due on a gift or other transfer of value.
items.changeNote: The 'Declaration' and ‘If you’re an agent’ section within 'How to fill in form IHT100a' has been updated as the page numbers are no longer required.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100a to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due on a trust, downloading it, opening it with the latest free Adobe Reader, completing it on‑screen and seeking support if it won’t open.
ai.whoAffected: Trustees and agents handling trusts for SME owners or self‑employed clients
actions: Download and save form IHT100a to your computer
Open the form using the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form does not open, contact online services support

items.title: HMRC email updates, videos and webinars for Self Assessment
items.description: Learn more about getting started with Self Assessment including registration, tax returns, tax bills and payments.
items.changeNote: Live webinar links have been added for 'New to Self Assessment — an introduction' and 'New to Self Assessment — records, budgeting and payments'. A new video link for 'Check if you need to pay tax on your cryptoassets' has been added.

ai.summary: HMRC provides email updates, webinars and videos covering all aspects of Self Assessment, from registration to filing, payments, and specific sections like self‑employment, property and foreign income. New live webinar links and a crypto‑assets video have been added.
ai.whoAffected: Self‑employed individuals, small business owners and anyone filing a Self Assessment tax return
actions: Advise clients to subscribe to the HMRC help and support email service for updates
Recommend relevant live or recorded webinars based on the client’s situation (e.g., self‑employment, property, foreign income)
Direct clients to specific YouTube videos that explain registration, budgeting, filing and payment processes
Assist clients in setting up budgeting or payment plans using the guidance videos and HMRC app

items.title: Claim a tax refund on your pension by post
items.description: Find out how to claim a tax refund on an additional lump sum or cash payment your private pension.

ai.summary: If you’ve overpaid tax on a private pension lump sum or cash payment, you can claim a refund by selecting the correct HMRC form, completing it by hand and posting it. HMRC will then repay any due amount via Faster Payments.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals who have received a pension lump sum or cash payment and may have paid too much tax, including those who have stopped work or flexibly accessed their pension
actions: Use the online tool or guidance to identify the correct form (e.g., P50Z, P53, P55) for the client’s pension payment type
Print the identified form
Complete the form by hand with the client’s details and tax information
Post the completed form to the HMRC address shown on the form

items.title: Changes to accounting for VAT for Northern Ireland and Great Britain from 1 January 2021
items.description: This guidance gives information about when you can, or need to, account for VAT on your tax return if you're a UK VAT-registered business.
items.changeNote: References to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' have been removed and replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: The Windsor Framework keeps Northern Ireland aligned with EU VAT rules for goods while remaining in the UK VAT system, including services, with HMRC still collecting revenues.
ai.whoAffected: UK VAT‑registered businesses, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and the self‑employed, that trade goods to, from or within Northern Ireland or provide services involving Northern Ireland
actions: Check client VAT accounting for goods moving to, from or within Northern Ireland follows the EU‑aligned administrative processes
Confirm that services transactions with Northern Ireland are treated as UK VAT transactions
Update client guidance and VAT return templates to reflect the continued UK alignment and HMRC collection role
Notify clients of the change from the Northern Ireland Protocol to the Windsor Framework and its impact on VAT accounting

items.title: Claim VAT refunds in Northern Ireland or the EU, if you’re established in Northern Ireland or in the EU
items.description: Find out how Northern Ireland and EU businesses can claim refunds of VAT incurred on goods in the EU and Northern Ireland using the EU VAT refund system.
items.changeNote: References to 'Northern Ireland Protocol' have been replaced by 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: Northern Ireland and EU businesses can claim VAT refunds on goods through the electronic cross‑border system under the Windsor Framework, provided they’re not established in the refund country and meet the eligibility rules.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses established in Northern Ireland or an EU member state (and their authorised agents) that have incurred VAT on goods in the other jurisdiction and have no fixed establishment, seat of economic activity or place of business in the refund country.
actions: Confirm the client is a taxable person established in NI or an EU state with a valid VAT number and no registration or fixed establishment in the refund country.
Check the claim relates only to goods, meets the minimum claim amounts (€400 for <1 year periods, €50 for full‑year periods) and falls within the 3‑month to 1‑year period limits.
Prepare the electronic claim using all mandatory standard fields and required invoice details, applying the correct expenditure codes.
Submit the completed claim by 30 September of the year following the refund period and keep supporting documentation for any queries.

items.title: VAT on movements of goods between Northern Ireland and the EU
items.description: How to charge and account for VAT on the movement of goods between Northern Ireland and EU member states (VAT Notice 725).
items.changeNote: References to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' have been removed and replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: The notice explains how VAT is charged and accounted for on goods moving between Northern Ireland and EU states under the Windsor Framework, including zero‑rating on dispatch, acquisition VAT by the customer, reporting requirements and special rules for own‑goods transfers and Intrastat.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that move goods between Northern Ireland and EU member states, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed traders.
ai.effectiveDate: 1 July 2021 (distance‑selling changes) and 1 January 2023 (VAT interest changes)
actions: Determine if the client supplies goods to VAT‑registered customers in the EU and apply the zero‑rate on dispatch from NI
Ensure the EU customer accounts for acquisition VAT on their return
Include the supplies on the client’s VAT return, EC Sales List and Intrastat filings using the correct tax point
If the client’s EU trade exceeds the Intrastat threshold, complete Supplementary Declarations
legislationRefs: Value Added Tax Act 1994, Schedules 9ZA and 9ZD

items.title: Check how to report and pay VAT on distance sales of goods from Northern Ireland to the EU
items.description: How to report and pay VAT due on the distance sales of goods from Northern Ireland to consumers in the EU using the One Stop Shop (OSS) Union scheme.
items.changeNote: The reference to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' has been replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: Northern Irish businesses selling goods to EU consumers that exceed the distance‑selling threshold must account for VAT in the consumer’s country, but can use the OSS Union scheme to file a single return. Those below the UK VAT threshold must first register for UK VAT to join OSS.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses in Northern Ireland (including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed) that sell goods to EU consumers, whether above or below the UK VAT registration threshold.
actions: Check eligibility: sales to EU consumers above the distance‑selling threshold and under the Windsor Framework
If turnover is below the UK VAT threshold, register for UK VAT and select activity code 63990 when registering
Register for the OSS Union scheme and complete the OSS return
Keep all required records for 10 years and submit OSS returns and payments as required
legislationRefs: 63990 Distance sales of goods (below UK VAT threshold)

items.title: Inheritance Tax: claim for relief — loss on sale of land (IHT38)
items.description: Use form IHT38 to claim relief on Inheritance Tax if you sell land or buildings from the deceased’s estate at a loss.
items.changeNote: Details on when to use the form IHT38 have been updated.

ai.summary: Use form IHT38 to claim Inheritance Tax relief when land or buildings from a deceased’s estate are sold at a loss, provided the sale occurs within the permitted period (usually 3 years, up to 4 years in some cases) and the claim is made by the person liable for the tax.
ai.whoAffected: The person liable for the Inheritance Tax on the property (e.g., executor or administrator of the deceased’s estate)
actions: Identify any qualifying loss sale of land or buildings within the permitted period after death
Confirm who is liable for the Inheritance Tax on the property
Complete form IHT38 with the required details
Submit the IHT38 claim to HMRC within the applicable time limit

items.title: Tell HMRC about assets previously held in an ‘18 to 25’ trust (IHT100h)
items.description: Report Inheritance Tax due on assets that have stopped being held in an ‘18 to 25’ trust using form IHT100h.
items.changeNote: The 'Declaration' section of 'How to fill in form IHT100h' has been updated.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100h to report Inheritance Tax due on an ‘18 to 25’ trust, downloading it, opening with Adobe Reader, completing on‑screen, and seeking support if it won’t open.
ai.whoAffected: Anyone who needs to report Inheritance Tax due on an ‘18 to 25’ trust
actions: Download and save form IHT100h
Open the form with the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form won’t open, contact online services support or read the accessibility statement

items.title: Tell HMRC about the end of a qualifying interest in possession because someone has died (IHT100b (death))
items.description: Use this form to tell us that a beneficiary's qualifying interest in possession in a trust has come to an end due to their death and Inheritance Tax is due.
items.changeNote: The declaration section wording has been updated to remove page specific references and clarify the statements that agents and trustees must provide.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100b (death) to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due when a beneficiary’s qualifying interest in possession ends because of death, by downloading, opening in Adobe Reader and completing it on‑screen.
ai.whoAffected: Beneficiaries whose qualifying interest in possession in a trust ends on death and the trustees/agents responsible for the trust
actions: Download form IHT100b (death) and save it to your computer
Open the saved form using the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form will not open, contact online services support for assistance

items.title: Edition 7: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — software developer newsletter
items.description: HMRC's newsletter for software developers for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.

ai.summary: HMRC’s newsletter updates software developers on Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, covering recent changes, service performance and required developer actions. Next edition due October 2026.
ai.whoAffected: Software developers creating MTD for Income Tax solutions
actions: Not stated in source

items.title: How model assisted valuation delivers large-scale property valuations
items.description: How the Valuation Office Agency uses model assisted valuation and mass appraisal to support large-scale valuation.
items.changeNote: Added PDF 'A Gaussian Markov Random Field model for the valuation of domestic properties in Wales, UK, using INLA'.

ai.summary: The Valuation Office Agency uses a model‑assisted valuation (AVM) and mass appraisal to value 1.5 million Welsh domestic properties for a 2028 Council Tax revaluation, with valuers checking data, targeting band margins and allowing customers to challenge their band.
