ai.whoAffected: Property owners in Wales subject to Council Tax, including SMEs and self‑employed individuals with domestic property holdings.
actions: Explain to clients that the VOA’s AVM determines Council Tax bands and that they have a legal right to challenge a band if they disagree
Advise clients to keep accurate property data and records in case valuers sample their property for review
Monitor VOA publications for model specifications, technical papers and external assessment reports to stay informed
Assist clients in preparing evidence and submitting challenges if their property is flagged at band margins or shows unusual valuation changes

items.title: Pay your Economic Crime Levy
items.description: How to pay the Economic Crime Levy, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Information about the bands for financial years from 1 April 2026 have been added.

ai.summary: The Economic Crime Levy must be paid by 30 Sept each year; rates depend on UK revenue bands, with small entities exempt and larger entities paying fixed amounts. Returns need a 14‑character reference, and payments can be made online, by Direct Debit, card or bank transfer, ensuring funds arrive before the deadline.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses with UK revenue over £10.2 million (band A, B, C, D) that are liable for the Economic Crime Levy, as well as any entity that must submit a levy return.
actions: Determine the client’s revenue band for the financial year and calculate the levy due
Obtain the 14‑character Economic Crime Levy return number and submit the return before the deadline
Arrange payment (online, Direct Debit, card or bank transfer) so it reaches HMRC by 30 Sept, accounting for bank processing times
Check for any partial‑year reductions or over‑payments and advise on refunds where applicable

items.title: Submit a return for the Economic Crime Levy
items.description: Find out how to submit a return and how to amend a return for the Economic Crime Levy.
items.changeNote: The example for who must submit a return has been updated from 'medium-sized entity' to 'band A entity'.

ai.summary: Registered businesses must file an Economic Crime Levy return each year by 30 September, even if they fall below the levy threshold, providing UK revenue, AML activity duration and the return preparer’s details, using the online service and keeping records for possible amendments or penalties.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that have registered for the Economic Crime Levy, including band A entities and any entity meeting the levy threshold
actions: Confirm the client is registered for the Economic Crime Levy and has a sign‑in for each entity
Collect the client’s UK revenue, AML activity period and preparer’s name, role and contact details for the accounting period
Submit the return online by 30 September and note the 14‑digit return number for payment
If needed, advise the client how to amend the return via their account and handle any refunds or penalties

items.title: Tax-free savings newsletter 23
items.description: September 2026 newsletter to update stakeholders on the latest news for tax-free savings.

ai.summary: HMRC’s newsletter outlines upcoming ISA rule reforms, guidance on reporting Lifetime ISA transfers and a user research programme for its digital ISA service.
ai.whoAffected: ISA managers and Child Trust Fund providers
actions: Track the announced ISA rule reforms and assess impact on client advice
Implement procedures to ensure accurate reporting of Lifetime ISA transfers
Prepare to engage in HMRC’s digital ISA service user research
Update client communications to reflect any changes in ISA guidance

items.title: Compliance checks: general information about compliance checks into large and complex businesses — CC/FS1c
items.description: Find out about the compliance checks HMRC carries out on certain large, complex businesses and their tax affairs.
items.changeNote: This factsheet has been updated to include Plastic Packaging Tax, Vaping Product Duty and Vaping Duty Stamps Scheme.

ai.summary: The factsheet gives guidance on HMRC compliance checks for large, complex businesses and their tax affairs.
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source

items.title: Negligible value claims and agreements
items.description: How to make a negligible value claim for unquoted shares, and how to check if shares previously quoted on the London Stock Exchange now have negligible value.
items.changeNote: HMRC's list of shares which have been declared as being worth negligible value is now valid up to and including 31 August 2026.

ai.summary: Negligible value claims let owners of assets that have fallen to almost no value realise a loss against CGT. Claims can be made by writing to the tax office or via Self Assessment. HMRC’s list shows previously LSE‑quoted shares deemed negligible up to 31 Aug 2026; unquoted or AIM companies aren’t listed.
ai.whoAffected: Owners of unquoted shares that have become worthless, shareholders of companies previously quoted on the London Stock Exchange, and directors of companies in liquidation or receivership – including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses with such shareholdings.
actions: Check the HMRC Negligible Value Agreement list to see if the share is listed as negligible
Gather evidence – statement of affairs, liquidator/receiver letter, balance‑sheet showing debts exceed assets, and proof no rescue is likely
Submit a claim by writing to your tax office or entering the negligible value on your Self Assessment return
If the company is in liquidation or receivership, include all required documents listed in the guidance

items.title: Provide or update your partnership details for VAT
items.description: Use form VAT2 to tell HMRC about a new partnership or update partner details.

ai.summary: Use form VAT2 to give HMRC partner details when registering for VAT, updating partners, adding/removing partners, or changing the partnership’s bank account; up to 8 partners per form, extra forms needed for more.
ai.whoAffected: Partnerships that need to register for VAT or update partner information, including adding/removing partners or changing bank details
actions: Collect the VAT registration number, business name, and each partner’s date of birth, NI number and signature
Complete a VAT2 form (one per up to 8 partners) and state the reason for sending
Upload the form via the VAT registration portal or post it to the VAT registration applications and changes team
Tell the client to await HMRC’s outcome notification by post or in their business tax account

items.title: Residence and foreign income and gains (FIG) regime etc (Self Assessment SA109)
items.description: Use supplementary pages SA109 to record your residence and domicile status on your SA100 Tax Return.
items.changeNote: The notes for the 2025 to 2026 tax year have been updated. References to a source-by-source basis have been removed from the notes of boxes 28 and 29 on page 9.

ai.summary: SA109 pages must be filed with the SA100 to record residence/domicile status and claim personal allowances for non‑UK residents. Use related helpsheets (HS264, HS300, HS302, HS303, HS304) for remittance basis, non‑resident income, dual residency and tax relief.
ai.whoAffected: Non‑UK resident individuals, including self‑employed people and owners of SMEs, who need to submit a UK Self Assessment return
actions: Determine the taxpayer’s residence and domicile status
Complete the SA109 supplementary pages and attach them to the SA100 return
Claim any personal allowances available to non‑UK residents on the SA109
Refer to the appropriate helpsheets (HS264, HS300, HS302, HS303, HS304) for specific issues such as remittance basis or dual residency

items.title: How to get an agent reference number for PAYE
items.description: Find out how to get an agent reference number for PAYE, Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) or Employment Related Securities (ERS), if you are a PAYE agent or payroll bureau.
items.changeNote: Made it clearer that this service is only for PAYE agents or payroll bureaus.

ai.summary: PAYE agents or payroll bureaus must apply online for an agent reference number, first checking if they need to register as a tax adviser, then using an agent services account to enrol PAYE, CIS and ERS services.
ai.whoAffected: PAYE agents, payroll bureaus and anyone needing to register as a tax adviser to use HMRC agent services
actions: Check whether you need to register as a tax adviser
If required, apply for an agent services account
Apply online for an agent reference number (provide full name, trading name, phone and email)
Sign into HMRC online services and enrol the PAYE, CIS and/or ERS services

items.title: Using software to file your company's information
items.description: How to send information to Companies House using commercial software.
items.changeNote: Updated call to action about filing accounts using software.

ai.summary: From 1 April 2028 all companies must file accounts via commercial software using iXBRL; web and paper filing will close. This applies to firms filing themselves or through accountants, requiring authentication codes, presenter accounts and, if fees apply, a credit account.
ai.whoAffected: All UK companies that file annual accounts, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed directors, whether they file directly or use an accountant
actions: Check each client’s current software can produce iXBRL and ZIP files for filing
Advise clients to obtain a company authentication code, presenter account and, if needed, a Companies House credit account
Recommend suitable commercial software and plan migration before the 1 April 2028 deadline
Confirm that any appointed accountants are ready to file using the new software requirements

items.title: Change the details of a UK establishment of an overseas company (OS CH01)
items.description: Use this form OS CH01 to change the details of a UK establishment of an overseas company.
items.changeNote: The address must be the UK establishment address. This means the physical location in the UK where the overseas company is carrying out its business.

ai.summary: Use form OS CH01 to notify Companies House of any changes to a UK establishment of an overseas company, ensuring the UK establishment address is provided and nationalities/countries are selected from the approved list.
ai.whoAffected: UK establishment of an overseas company (overseas companies operating in the UK)
actions: Confirm the client’s UK establishment address is the physical location where business is carried out
Complete OS CH01, entering the address exactly as the UK establishment address
Select nationalities and countries only from the official standard list provided
Submit the completed OS CH01 form to Companies House

items.title: Company authentication codes for online filing
items.description: How to request and manage the company authentication code you'll need to file information online at Companies House.
items.changeNote: Overseas companies can now request an authentication code using the Find and update company information service.

ai.summary: A 6‑digit alphanumeric company authentication code authorises online filings. Request via Companies House WebFiling (UK) or Find and update service (overseas); it’s sent by post, not email or phone. Keep it secure, change if compromised, and inform anyone filing for the company of any changes.
ai.whoAffected: All UK‑registered companies, overseas companies with a UK establishment, their directors, accountants and anyone filing online on their behalf.
actions: Advise clients to request their code early via WebFiling or Find and update service and allow up to 10 working days for delivery.
Ensure clients store the code securely and treat it like a bank PIN.
Prompt clients to inform you of any code changes and update your records accordingly.
Warn overseas clients they must use Find and update service and can only file package accounts.

items.title: Overseas companies in the UK: registration and filing
items.description: Registration and filing obligations of an overseas company that opens an establishment in the UK.
items.changeNote: Overseas companies can now file iXBRL package accounts online.

ai.summary: The guide outlines how overseas companies (including those from the EEA) must register a UK establishment, the documents to file with Companies House, and ongoing accounting, naming and trading disclosure duties, now using online iXBRL filing.
ai.whoAffected: Overseas companies opening or already operating a UK establishment, including those from the EEA, and advisers to such companies
actions: Confirm the client is an overseas (or EEA) company planning a UK establishment
Register the establishment with Companies House and submit the required documents
Prepare iXBRL package accounts and file them online, complying with accounting, name and trading disclosure rules
Maintain ongoing filing and disclosure obligations after registration

items.title: Companies House fees
items.description: A list of all the fees Companies House charges, and how we determine these fees.
items.changeNote: Added the £50 fee for filing overseas company package accounts online.

ai.summary: Companies House fees are set by specific statutory fee regulations and cost‑recovery principles, with a 3.5% cost of capital and no cross‑subsidy. Some documents under the Companies Act 1985 or NI Order 1986 are free, and fees may change as announced.
ai.whoAffected: All companies, overseas companies, LLPs, limited partnerships and other entities filing documents with Companies House, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Check if client filings fall under the Companies Act 1985 or the Companies (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 to qualify for free filing
Identify the applicable statutory fee regulations for each filing type and advise on the correct fee
Explain to clients that fees reflect full cost recovery, including a 3.5% cost of capital, and that no cross‑subsidy occurs
Monitor Companies House guidance for any announced fee changes and update client advice accordingly
legislationRefs: The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (Companies, Overseas Companies and Limited Liability Partnerships) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1907) as amended by The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations 2016 (SI 2016/621)

The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (European Economic Interest Grouping and European Public Limited-Liability Company) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1908) as amended by The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations 2016 (SI 2016/621)

The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (Limited Partnerships and Newspaper Proprietors) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009/2392) as amended by The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (Limited Partnerships) (Amendment) Regulations 2011 (SI 2011/319) and The Registrar of Companies (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations 2016 (SI 2016/621)

items.title: Compliance checks: The Human Rights Act and penalties for breaches of the prohibition of promotion of certain tax avoidance arrangements (POP) legislation — CC/FS92
items.description: This factsheet tells you about your rights if HMRC is considering charging you a penalty under the prohibition of promotion of certain tax avoidance arrangements rules.

ai.summary: The factsheet states it is guidance only and reflects HMRC’s position at the time of writing.
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source

items.title: Tell HMRC about a transferor or settlor who is not a long-term UK resident (D31a)
items.description: Use this form to tell HMRC about a transferor or settlor who is not a long-term UK resident.  This form is for chargeable events on or after 6 April 2025.
items.changeNote: Form 'Long-term UK residence (D31a)' has been updated.

ai.summary: Use form D31a with a completed IHT100 to report non‑UK resident transferors or settlors for chargeable events from 6 April 2025; download, open in Adobe Reader and complete on‑screen.
ai.whoAffected: Transferors or settlors who are not long‑term UK residents (and their advisers)
actions: Ensure a completed IHT100 (IHT100a‑IHT100h) is filed alongside D31a
Download the D31a form and save it locally
Open the form with the latest free version of Adobe Reader and complete it on‑screen
If the form won’t open, contact online services support

items.title: Pension schemes newsletter 185 — September 2026
items.description: Newsletter 185, published by HMRC in September 2026 to update stakeholders on the latest news for pension schemes.

ai.summary: HMRC’s newsletter outlines updates on wound‑up scheme returns, lump‑sum death benefits, migration from the closed online service and relief‑at‑source for pension schemes.
ai.whoAffected: Pension scheme trustees and administrators (stakeholders)
actions: Review any wound‑up scheme return obligations
Check client processes for lump‑sum death benefits
Assist clients in migrating pension schemes from the closed online service
Confirm relief‑at‑source arrangements are correct

items.title: Almost 3 million young adults are ‘quids in’ after claiming Child Trust Fund
items.description: Young people urged to go online to find their Child Trust Fund.

ai.summary: Nearly 3 million matured Child Trust Funds have been claimed or moved to ISAs, but about 827,000 remain unclaimed, averaging £2,310 each. Young adults can locate their accounts for free via the GOV.UK tool using their NI number and DOB, then choose to withdraw, keep, or transfer the money.
ai.whoAffected: Young adults aged 18‑24 with matured Child Trust Funds, and their parents or guardians
actions: Guide clients to use the GOV.UK Child Trust Fund locator tool with their NI number and date of birth
Advise clients on the three options: withdraw, keep the fund, or transfer to an ISA
Help clients gather required details (NI number, DOB) and submit the request, noting the ~3‑week response time
Inform clients of the average value and encourage timely claim to avoid funds remaining unclaimed

items.title: Claim personal allowances and tax refunds if you live abroad (R43)
items.description: How to claim a refund on tax and personal allowances on UK income if you're not resident in the UK on form R43.
items.changeNote: The personal allowances and tax repayments (R43) form and guidance notes have been updated to reflect the changes to the Double Taxation Agreement between the UK and Israel by the 2019 Protocol which entered into force on 28 October 2019.

ai.summary: Non‑resident individuals can claim UK personal allowances and tax refunds for UK income from the current year and the previous four years using form R43, unless they already file a Self Assessment or have rental income over £2,500.
ai.whoAffected: UK non‑resident individuals who receive UK income such as property rent, pensions, dividends, interest or state benefits and are not already filing a Self Assessment.
actions: Verify the client’s residency status and days spent in the UK
Determine if a tax certificate is required and obtain it
Gather details of all UK income for the relevant tax year(s)
Submit form R43 online or download the PDF and post it, unless rental income exceeds £2,500 – then advise filing a Self Assessment

items.title: How to prove your identity for Companies House at the Post Office
items.description: How to complete your identity verification in person at a Post Office, once you've entered your photo ID details online.
items.changeNote: Added 'Deadline' guidance. You have 21 days from the date you booked the Post Office appointment to complete the verification process and view your result.

ai.summary: Clients must enter photo ID details online, download a customer letter, visit a Post Office with the letter and original ID within 21 days, have their QR code scanned and photo taken, then await the result email to obtain their Companies House personal code.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals needing to verify their identity for Companies House (e.g., directors, company officers)
actions: Advise the client to enter their photo‑ID details via the Companies House online service and book a Post Office appointment.
Tell the client to download the customer letter and keep their original photo ID ready for the visit.
Ensure the client attends any eligible Post Office within 21 days, where staff will scan the QR code and capture their photo and ID.
Follow up to confirm the client receives the GOV.UK One Login email with their personal code or advise next steps if the check fails.

items.title: Submit an enquiry to HM Treasury
items.description: Use this form to send an enquiry to HM Treasury.

items.title: Trader Support Service users urged to prepare for new platform
items.description: Businesses should prepare now before switchover to continue trading.

ai.summary: The free Trader Support Service will move to a new digital platform next month; all goods movements between Great Britain and Northern Ireland must be submitted on it from 20 October. Businesses must pre‑enrol after receiving an invitation email (from 1 October) and update their details to avoid disruption.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses registered for the Trader Support Service that move goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland
actions: Watch for the HMRC invitation email (starting 1 October) and pre‑enrol on the new TSS platform before 20 October
Use the test environment to become familiar with the new system and create a new password
Check and update business details and permissions on the new platform
Ensure the updated profile is saved so declarations can be submitted after 20 October

items.title: Producing Dovey Native Botanical Gin
items.description: Find out how to apply to the Spirit Drinks Verification Scheme, pay fees and comply with the product specification for Dovey Native Botanical Gin.
items.changeNote: Information about the transitional arrangements for existing producers of Dovey Native Botanical Gin has been removed as the arrangement ended on 1 September 2026.

ai.summary: New producers must apply to the Spirit Drinks Verification Scheme, pay fees, undergo verification visits every two years and stay compliant to market Dovey Native Botanical Gin legally.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals planning to produce and market Dovey Native Botanical Gin, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed producers
actions: Apply to the Spirit Drinks Verification Scheme before starting production
Pay the registration and verification fees when invoiced
Prepare documentation, equipment and procedures for the verification visit
If non‑compliant, implement changes within the agreed timeframe and inform customers if verification is withdrawn

items.title: National Minimum Wage information for employers
items.description: Find out about the checks we carry out to make sure you're paying your workers at least the National Minimum Wage.
items.changeNote: In 'About National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage checks — NMW FS1', references to the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) have been updated to the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST).’

ai.summary: The factsheet outlines HMRC’s checks to ensure employers pay at least the National Minimum or Living Wage, how to self‑review payroll records, details on arrears, penalties and tribunal video witness procedures.
ai.whoAffected: Employers who pay workers the National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage, including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses
actions: Conduct a self‑review of payroll records against NMW/NLW rates
Verify all workers receive at least the applicable minimum wage
Identify and address any NMW arrears to avoid penalties
Prepare for possible tribunal hearings, including video witness arrangements

items.title: Pay Stamp Duty Reserve Tax
items.description: How to pay your Stamp Duty Reserve Tax, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: SDRT is due on paperless share purchases. CREST trades are auto‑deducted; off‑market trades need a written notice with buyer/seller details, securities info, payment reference and must be paid within 14 days or by the 7th of the following month. Use correct reference and HMRC bank details.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals who buy or sell shares, especially those making off‑market share transactions
actions: Send a written notice for off‑market share trades including buyer/seller details, securities transferred, reliefs claimed, payment details and a reference number you choose
Ensure the notice and payment reach HMRC within the applicable deadline – 14 days for CREST‑eligible trades or the 7th of the month after the agreement for non‑CREST trades
Use the correct reference number; if an error occurs, contact SDRT enquiries to have the payment moved to the right tax bill
Pay electronically using the UK or overseas HMRC account details provided and allow the appropriate processing time (same/next day for CHAPS/Faster Payments, 3 working days for Bacs)

items.title: Valuation scales 2026
items.description: Find the 2026 valuation scales that the Valuation Office uses to value different parts of business properties depending on its floor level and how it's used.
items.changeNote: 'Offices modern standard with lift - London Docklands' has been replaced because the LAB accommodation use code has changed and 'Padel and tennis centres' has been added.

ai.summary: The 2026 valuation scales set relative values for parts of business properties based on floor level and use, with different scales for categories like central London offices versus other areas.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that own, lease or occupy commercial property, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed property owners
actions: Identify each client’s property type and floor level to match the correct valuation scale
Determine if the property falls under multiple scales (e.g., central London office) and select the appropriate one
Apply the 2026 relative values when calculating business rates or tax liabilities
Update client records and advice notes with the new scale information

items.title: More than £300 million paid out through Help to Save with thousands more savers set to benefit
items.description: Low income earners encouraged to open a Help to Save account in UK Savings Week.

ai.summary: Help to Save, a government scheme giving low‑income earners a 50% bonus on savings up to £2,400, has paid out over £300 million. Eligibility expands in 2028 to all Universal Credit claimants and removes caring‑responsibility earnings test, adding about 1.5 million households. The scheme is now permanent.
ai.whoAffected: Low‑income earners, Universal Credit claimants, people with caring responsibilities, and their employers or advisors
actions: Notify eligible clients about the 2028 eligibility expansion and permanent status
Help clients check eligibility and open accounts via GOV.UK or the HMRC app
Advise clients to save £1‑£50 each month to maximise the 50% bonus

Apply the guidance in client advice where relevant

items.title: Inheritance Tax: jointly owned assets (IHT404)
items.description: Use the IHT404 with form IHT400 to give details of all UK assets the deceased owned jointly with another person.
items.changeNote: Schedule IHT404 has been updated to make it clearer where to enter spouse and charity exemption amounts.

ai.whoAffected: Personal representatives, accountants and advisors handling estates where the deceased held jointly‑owned UK assets
actions: Obtain Schedule IHT404 and the IHT400 estate return
Record all jointly‑owned UK assets on IHT404 as part of the IHT400 filing
Enter spouse and charity exemption amounts as clarified in the updated schedule
Submit the completed IHT404 with the IHT400 return to HMRC

items.title: Report Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) contractor monthly return errors if you've received a letter from HMRC
items.description: Tell HMRC about an error if they’ve sent you a letter about applying an incorrect rate to your subcontractor payments in tax year 2025 to 2026.

ai.summary: HMRC letters indicate possible incorrect CIS rates for subcontractor payments in tax year 2025‑26. Contractors must report the error via the online CIS disclosure form, providing business details, UTR, letter reference and any underpaid tax. HMRC will review and respond within 28 working days.
ai.whoAffected: CIS contractors who have received an HMRC letter about an incorrect rate, including individuals, designated company members, trustees, estate representatives and authorised agents.
actions: Identify clients who received the HMRC letter about a CIS rate error
Use the HMRC CIS online service to complete the disclosure form
Gather required information: business name, UTR, letter reference (CFSS), and underpaid tax details
Submit the form and advise the client to await HMRC’s decision (usually within 28 working days)

items.title: Reduction in the cash Individual Savings Account (ISA) limit
items.description: This tax information and impact note is about changes to Individual Savings Account  (ISA) regulations to reduce the annual subscription limit of cash ISAs.

ai.summary: The cash ISA annual subscription limit for people under 65 is reduced to £12,000 starting 6 April 2027, via changes to the Individual Savings Account Regulations 1998.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals aged under 65, including SME owners, partners and the self‑employed.
actions: Inform clients that the cash ISA limit will fall to £12,000 from 6 April 2027.
Review existing cash ISA contributions to ensure they do not exceed the new limit.
Discuss alternative tax‑efficient savings options if clients need to save more.
Update client records and advice notes to reflect the regulatory change.

items.title: Directors warned to verify identities with Companies House following first Insolvency Service prosecutions
items.description: Court action highlights legal duty on directors to complete identity verification

ai.summary: Directors must verify their identity with Companies House or face prosecution. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 requires new directors to verify by 18 Nov 2025 and existing directors to do so within 12 months when filing their next confirmation statement. Recent fines show enforcement is active.
ai.whoAffected: Company directors (newly appointed and existing) and firms with unverified directors
actions: Check client director registers for verification status
Advise clients to complete identity verification online via Companies House or an authorised provider
Ensure the next confirmation statement is filed on time and includes verification
Monitor ongoing compliance and keep records to avoid prosecution
legislationRefs: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023

items.title: Change your company accounting reference date (AA01)
items.description: Use this form to change an accounting reference date relating to either the current or immediately previous accounting period.
items.changeNote: Added wording for overseas companies with a UK establishment. They must send the paper form by post to the correct Companies House office.

ai.summary: Companies can change their accounting reference date using form AA01, must submit within the filing window, preferably online; overseas companies with UK establishments must post the paper form, and confirmation letters are no longer sent—check the new date online.
ai.whoAffected: Companies (including overseas companies with a UK establishment) that need to change their accounting reference date
actions: Advise the client to use the online service to submit the AA01 form for a quicker update
Ensure the submission is made within the period allowed for laying and delivering accounts for the current or immediately previous period
If the client is an overseas company with a UK establishment, instruct them to send the paper form by post to the correct Companies House office
Tell the client to search Companies House after filing to verify the new accounting reference date

items.title: Agents, Small and Mid-Sized Businesses Customer Survey 2025

items.title: Verify your child for the childcare service
items.description: Use form CVF1 to verify your child for the childcare service.
items.changeNote: Information about the documents you need to send with form CVF1, to verify your child has been updated.

ai.summary: Use form CVF1 online to verify a child for childcare services, gathering a passport, birth or adoption certificate, and ensure a modern browser; submit the original document by post, not a photocopy.

Complete the CVF1 form in one session (no saving) using an up‑to‑date browser
Submit the completed form and the original document by post (no photocopies)
Advise clients to keep a copy of the posted documents for their records

items.title: Compliance checks: penalties for CIS payments or returns connected to deliberate non-compliance — CC/FS96
items.description: This factsheet tells you about the penalties we may charge if we’ve issued a determination under either section 62A or 62B of the Finance Act 2004 for the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS).

ai.summary: This factsheet explains when HMRC may impose penalties for CIS payments or returns linked to deliberate non‑compliance, how penalties are calculated, notification methods, officer liability and your rights during the penalty process.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals making Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) payments or returns
actions: Check client CIS payments and returns for compliance with CIS rules
Maintain full records to support any HMRC calculations
Inform company officers of potential personal liability for CIS penalties
Promptly respond to any HMRC communication about possible penalties

items.title: Claim compensation for Childcare service issues
items.description: Check if you can get compensation if you’ve been unable to access Tax-Free Childcare or free childcare for working parents due to technical issues.
items.changeNote: 'What to do after you get compensation' section updated, as tax credit changes can no longer be reported to HMRC.

ai.summary: Parents who faced technical problems with the Childcare online service and missed Tax-Free Childcare top‑up or free childcare can claim compensation by completing an online form or writing to HMRC, providing proof of payments and account details. Universal Credit recipients must report any compensation to DWP.
ai.whoAffected: Parents who use Tax-Free Childcare or free childcare for working parents and have paid for childcare they should have received free
actions: Identify clients who experienced technical issues and paid for childcare
Help them complete the online form for Tax-Free Childcare top‑up and print/post it to HMRC
Assist clients to draft and send a letter with required details to the Childcare Service address for free childcare compensation
Advise Universal Credit claimants to report any compensation received to the Department for Work and Pensions

items.title: Hundreds of new officers to hunt down dirty money networks
items.description: Five hundred new officers to be recruited in a £500 million crackdown on money laundering, as part of the government's Anti-Money Laundering and Asset Recovery Strategy.

ai.summary: The government will recruit 500 new officers, funded by £500 million, to target money‑laundering networks, seize criminal assets and strengthen AML supervision across police, NCA, CPS and professional services.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed professionals, especially those in retail, hospitality and financial services that may face tighter AML supervision and scrutiny of high‑street premises
actions: Review client AML policies and ensure they meet the heightened supervision standards highlighted in the new strategy
Update record‑keeping and suspicious activity reporting procedures for clients in affected sectors
Advise high‑street retail and service clients on compliance to avoid being classified as ‘dodgy’ shops
Monitor guidance from the FCA, NCA and SFO for any new compliance requirements and relay updates to clients

items.title: The Finance Act 2026 (Scottish and Welsh Property Income Rates) (Appointed Day and Tax Year) Regulations 2026
items.description: The Regulations appoint 16th September 2026 as the day on which section 8 of, and Schedule 2 to, the Finance Act 2026 come into force. They also appoint the tax year 2027-28 as the first tax year in relation to which the amendments made by section 8 and Schedule 2 have effect. Those amendments accordingly have effect for the tax year 2027-28 and subsequent tax years.

items.title: Almost 7 million adults in the dark about their State Pension
items.description: HMRC is encouraging people to check their State Pension forecast using the HMRC app during Pension Awareness Week.

ai.summary: HMRC urges all adults, especially 45‑54‑year‑olds, to use the free HMRC app during Pension Awareness Week (15‑18 Sept 2026) to check their State Pension forecast, view NI gaps and top‑up contributions, and consult the Tax Confident site for retirement tax advice.
ai.whoAffected: All UK adults, particularly 45‑54‑year‑olds, including employees, self‑employed and owners of SMEs
actions: Notify clients of Pension Awareness Week (15‑18 Sept 2026) and the need to check their State Pension forecast
Help clients download and access the free HMRC app to view their forecast and NI record
Identify any NI gaps and advise on eligible top‑up contributions
Refer clients to HMRC’s Tax Confident website for retirement tax guidance

items.title: The Finance Act 2009 (Publishing Details of Deliberate Tax Defaulters: Increase to Threshold) Order 2026
items.description: Section 94 of the Finance Act 2009 provides for the Commissioners for HM Revenue and Customs to publish information (including names) of persons who have been penalised for deliberate defaults where the tax lost exceeds £25,000.

items.title: Being a company director
items.description: Understanding your role as director of a limited company and your responsibilities to Companies House.
items.changeNote: Added a section 'Scam offering money to become a company director'. This section explains what to do if a recruiter offers you money to provide your identity details and be named as a director for an unknown company.

ai.summary: Directors must file annual accounts, confirmation statements and any changes with Companies House, ensure tax returns, and avoid conflicts of interest. New scam warns against paid director offers; victims should not share details, report fraud, and resign using TM01 if appointed.
ai.whoAffected: Current and prospective company directors, especially in SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who may be named as directors
actions: Advise clients to register for Companies House email reminders and file accounts and confirmation statements on time
Ensure directors understand their duties under the Companies Act 2006, including reporting changes and avoiding conflicts of interest
Warn clients about scams offering money to become a director; instruct them not to share personal details and to report any offer to Report Fraud online or 0300 123 2040
If a client has been appointed to a fraudulent company, guide them to resign via form TM01, keep records of the resignation and seek independent legal advice

items.title: PAYE draft forms: P45
items.description: Find approved final versions of form P45 for PAYE software developers.
items.changeNote: The Design specification for P45 (Online), P45 (Continuous), P45 (Continuous)(E), P45 (Laser continuous), P45 (Laser sheet), and P45 manual forms have been updated. Information about Tax credits and Universal Credit has been removed.

actions: Identify if you are developing PAYE software that needs substitute P45 forms
Download the draft P45 forms from the GOV.UK source
Incorporate the draft designs into your software
Check that the generated forms meet HMRC specifications

items.title: Work out your qualifying income for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: Find out what counts as qualifying income from self-employment and property when using Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
items.changeNote: The information about what you should do if all your self-employment and property income ceased before 6 April 2026 has been updated.

ai.summary: Qualifying income is the total pre‑expense turnover from self‑employment and property, taken from the previous year’s Self Assessment return. It determines whether a client must use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, unless all such income stopped before 6 April 2026.
ai.whoAffected: Self‑employed individuals and property owners (including sole traders and owners of jointly owned property) who may need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
actions: Check the client’s qualifying income from self‑employment and property using the previous tax year’s Self Assessment return.
If the income exceeds the relevant threshold, ensure the client signs up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax and keeps digital records/quarterly updates.
If all self‑employment and property income ceased before 6 April 2026, advise the client to inform HMRC and file the final tax return showing income up to cessation.
If qualifying income falls below the threshold for three consecutive years, advise the client they may opt out of the service.

items.title: Check what to do if HMRC has signed you up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: If you’ve been contacted by HMRC telling you we have signed you up, find out what steps you need to take next.
items.changeNote: Guidance has been updated to confirm HMRC will also check records against the 2025 to 2026 tax return if it's already been submitted. It's also been updated to make clear what you should do if all your income sources ceased before, on or from 6 April 2026.

ai.summary: HMRC may automatically enrol sole traders and landlords with income over £50,000 into Making Tax Digital for Income Tax. Clients must confirm HMRC’s records, adopt compatible software, create digital records, send quarterly updates and file the tax return.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 in the 2024‑25 tax year, and any agents acting for them
actions: Check the client’s HMRC online account to confirm they have been signed up
Review and confirm the client’s income and expense details, adding new sources or noting ceased ones
Select and set up compatible MTDiT software to create digital records and send quarterly updates
Help the client catch up on any overdue quarterly updates and submit the 2026‑27 tax return

items.title: Simplified Process for Internal Market Movements (SPIMM): Category of goods guidance
items.description: Find out details about the different types of Category 1, Category 2 and Standard goods.
items.changeNote: Guidance has been amended to reflect the allowed use of I1 C&F and C21i EIDR NOP for Category 2 goods.

ai.summary: The Windsor Framework classifies GB‑to‑NI goods as Category 1, Category 2 or Standard, with Category 1 and 2 governed by Annex IX of the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee decision. Updated guidance now allows I1 C&F and C21i EIDR NOP for Category 2 goods.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that move goods from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and the self‑employed
actions: Determine whether each client’s goods are Category 1, Category 2 or Standard using the guidance
Review the specific requirements in Annex IX for Category 1 and Category 2 goods
Confirm that any Category 2 goods use the permitted I1 C&F and C21i EIDR NOP procedures
Advise clients to document compliance with the Windsor Framework requirements
legislationRefs: Annex IX of Decision of the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee on laying down arrangements relating to the Windsor Framework

items.title: Visitor levy in England
items.description: This consultation seeks views on the design of a new Mayoral power to create visitor levies on overnight stays in England.
items.changeNote: Government response to the consultation added.

ai.summary: The government proposes giving Mayoral Strategic Authorities in England power to introduce local overnight visitor levies, with consultation on extending this to Foundation Strategic Authorities, revenue use, covered accommodation types, rate calculation, liability, administration and equality impacts.
ai.whoAffected: Mayoral Strategic Authorities, Foundation Strategic Authorities, owners of accommodation businesses (e.g., hotels, B&Bs), and overnight visitors in England
actions: Monitor the consultation and note any upcoming legislative changes
Advise accommodation‑based SME clients on potential levy exposure and budgeting
Help clients develop systems to assess liability and record levy payments
Prepare guidance on how levy revenues might be used and any equality considerations

items.title: Anti‑avoidance information notices
items.description: Find out about anti-avoidance information notices (AAINs), including their purpose, how they work and the terms used in them.

ai.summary: Guidance explains how HMRC applies anti‑avoidance information notice legislation, their purpose, implications for recipients and the terminology used.
ai.whoAffected: Taxpayers who receive an anti‑avoidance information notice (you or your client)
actions: Read the AAIN carefully to understand its purpose
Explain to the client what the notice means for their tax position
Check how HMRC is applying the anti‑avoidance legislation
Clarify any specific terms used in the notice using the guidance

items.title: Improved Self Assessment registration service launched
items.description: Customers who have income to declare for the 2025 to 2026 tax year encouraged to register for Self Assessment now.

ai.summary: HMRC has launched an improved online Self Assessment registration service. New filers for 2025‑26 must register by 5 Oct 2026 to get a UTR and avoid penalties; existing filers must reactivate if needed. The system pre‑populates data and issues UTRs within 72 hours.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals who need to file a Self Assessment for the 2025‑26 tax year – including newly self‑employed, new partners, those with untaxed income over £2,500, and anyone with income to declare – as well as agents who still use paper forms.
actions: Use HMRC’s free online checking tool to confirm each client’s need to register
If registration is required, advise clients to register via GOV.UK by 5 Oct 2026 to obtain a UTR
Prompt clients who no longer need to file to notify HMRC immediately to avoid penalties
Check existing clients’ registration status and reactivate accounts where a 2025‑26 return is needed

items.title: Community and Amateur Sports Club newsletter 5 — September 2026
items.description: Use the newsletters to get HMRC updates if you're a charity or Community and Amateur Sports Club (CASC).

ai.summary: HMRC’s newsletter informs charities and Community and Amateur Sports Clubs about a new Gift Aid video, guidance reviews, Claim Gift Aid service enhancements, and internal system updates.
ai.whoAffected: Charities and Community and Amateur Sports Clubs (CASC)
actions: Watch the new HMRC Gift Aid video
Review the latest guidance updates
Check the enhanced Claim Gift Aid online service
Monitor any announced system changes

items.title: Charities newsletter 3 — September 2026
items.description: Get information about HMRC consultations, Gift Aid, guidance reviews and updates to charity services and systems.

ai.summary: HMRC’s newsletter reminds charities to keep their registration eligibility up‑to‑date and highlights new user research sessions, a Gift Aid video, guidance reviews and service updates.
ai.whoAffected: Registered charities and advisers who support them
actions: Review each charity client’s registration eligibility regularly
Encourage clients to sign up for HMRC user research sessions
Watch the new HMRC Gift Aid video and ensure clients’ Gift Aid processes match the guidance
Monitor HMRC guidance reviews and system updates for any changes affecting clients

items.title: Temporary zero rate of VAT for domestic electricity in Great Britain
items.description: This tax information and impact note is about a temporary zero rate of VAT for qualifying supplies of electricity in Great Britain.

ai.summary: A temporary zero VAT rate applies to qualifying domestic electricity supplies in Great Britain from 1 Oct 2026 to 31 Mar 2027; all other domestic fuels continue at 5% VAT across the UK.
ai.whoAffected: Households and electricity suppliers providing qualifying domestic electricity in Great Britain
actions: Update client VAT calculations to reflect 0% rate for domestic electricity during the period
Notify affected clients of the continued 5% VAT on other domestic fuels
Adjust invoicing templates and accounting software accordingly
Monitor the end date (31 March 2027) for re‑application of standard rates

items.title: The Value Added Tax (Supplies of Domestic Electricity) Order 2026
items.description: This Order introduces a temporary zero rate of VAT on supplies of domestic electricity in England and Wales and Scotland. The zero rate applies to supplies made in the period beginning with 1st October 2026 and ending with 31st March 2027 by modifying Schedule 8 (zero-rating) to the Value Added Tax Act 1994 (“VATA”) so it has effect as if it contained a new Group 24 which specifies the description

items.title: How to register your client for a tax service as an agent
items.description: Find out how to register your client for Self Assessment, Corporation Tax, PAYE, VAT or their trust or estate.
items.changeNote: Guidance on how to register your client for Self Assessment if they are  not self-employed has been updated.

ai.summary: Agents can register clients for Self Assessment, Corporation Tax, PAYE, VAT, trusts or estates via HMRC online or agent services accounts, using required IDs, agent codes and client details, with paper forms available for non‑online Self Assessment registrations.

items.title: Complete your Self Assessment tax return for the last tax year

ai.whoAffected: Individuals required to submit a Self Assessment tax return for the 2025‑26 tax year, such as employees, company directors, self‑employed, partners, landlords, clergy, MPs and other specific groups.

items.title: Self Assessment: Employment (SA102)
items.description: Use supplementary pages SA102 to record employment income on your SA100 Tax Return.

Check that all employment income is correctly recorded on the SA102 pages

items.title: Tell HMRC about an exit charge on assets in a trust (IHT100c)
items.description: Use this form to tell us that Inheritance Tax is due on an exit from a trust.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100c to notify HMRC that inheritance tax is due on a trust exit; download, open with Adobe Reader, complete on-screen, and contact support if it won’t open.

actions: Download the IHT100c form to your computer

items.title: Local reference rents, listed by BRMA and property size (August 2026)
items.description: Local reference rent (LRR) levels by number of rooms and broad rental market areas (BRMA) for residential properties in England in August 2026.

ai.summary: Local reference rent (LRR) levels for residential properties in England are published for August 2026, categorised by room type (CAT 1A‑1C) and Broad Rental Market Area (BRMA).

actions: Check the August 2026 LRR tables for the client’s BRMA and room category when advising on rent levels

Update any rent‑review advice to reflect the new LRR values
Refer to the Housing Benefit section of the Rent Officer Handbook for methodology

items.title: Download the HMRC app
items.description: Download and access the HMRC app to manage your details, taxes and benefits.
items.changeNote: Guidance about how you can use the HMRC app to manage your information, taxes and benefits has been added.

ai.summary: The HMRC app for iOS and Android lets users sign in with a PIN, fingerprint or facial recognition to view and update personal details, check tax codes, UTRs, NI records, make payments, set reminders, claim refunds and manage benefits like State Pension and Child Benefit.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals, including self‑employed persons and owners of small or medium enterprises who need to manage their tax, National Insurance and benefit information via HMRC online services.
actions: Advise clients to download the HMRC app and sign in using their existing HMRC online credentials or create new ones in the app
Encourage clients to update their name, address and contact preferences through the app’s Manage your information section
Show clients how to check tax codes, UTRs, NI gaps and make payments or set payment reminders via the app

items.title: Loan charge settlement scheme: how HMRC will implement it
items.description: Find out how HMRC will apply the loan charge settlement scheme to disguised remuneration loan charge liabilities.

ai.whoAffected: Individuals and employers with disguised remuneration loan charge liabilities, including SME owners, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Identify clients who have loan charge liabilities
Check the timing of HMRC settlement offers for each client
Inform clients of the settlement period they have to respond
Explain how the settlement amount is calculated and guide them through the process

items.title: Convert a UK societas to a public limited company (SE CV01)

Complete the form using the standard list of nationalities and countries
Prepare a £124 cheque or postal order payable to Companies House
Submit the completed form and payment to Companies House

items.title: Register a limited liability partnership (LL IN01)

items.title: Register a private or public company (IN01)

ai.whoAffected: Individuals or entities registering a private or public company, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed entrepreneurs.

items.title: Compliance checks: alternative dispute resolution — CC/FS21

items.title: Inheritance Tax account (IHT400)

items.description: This explanatory note sets out how the 2024-25 Income Tax data published by HMRC and population data published by the ONS is used to update the Scottish Government’s funding.

items.changeNote: The section 'When you can rely on information or advice given by HMRC' has been updated with information on when a clearance applies to you.

ai.summary: The Non‑Statutory Clearance Service lets clients request written HMRC advice on transactions where legislation is unclear, provided they have genuine uncertainty and have used all guidance. actions: Check whether the transaction is covered by a statutory clearance or another appropriate route before applying for non‑statutory clearance
Confirm the client has read all relevant guidance, cannot find the needed information and has a genuine uncertainty about the legislation
Prepare the application using the correct annex checklist (A‑E) and submit it to the specified email address, ensuring all information is accurate and complete

chapter INTM162000 of the International manual

items.title: How to avoid payslip fraud
items.description: Check that the tax and National Insurance shown on your payslip or deduction statement has been paid correctly if you’re an agency worker, temporary worker or contractor, or you work through an umbrella or payroll company.

ai.summary: Payslip fraud occurs when tax, NI or CIS deductions shown on a payslip aren’t paid to HMRC, risking benefits, State Pension and tax bills. actions: Advise clients to obtain a payslip for every pay period and verify personal, employer and tax‑code details
Instruct clients to compare tax and NI deductions on payslips with their Personal Tax Account, HMRC app, NI record or student loan account
Prompt clients to report any missing, false or mismatched payslips or CIS statements to HMRC promptly
For CIS sub‑contractors, ensure they include full invoice amounts and CIS deductions on their Self‑Assessment return and keep supporting evidence

items.description: GOV.UK One Login will become the main sign-in option for the Find and update company information service.
